And, on that note, we will be closing the blog for today.

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are on their way to Dublin to meet with Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy (18:04) after their talks with Russia’s Vladimir Putin in Moscow earlier today (14:16, 14:41, 17:28, 17:49).

During the meeting, the leaders discussed Russia’s key demands when it comes to the peace process and agreed to hold another round of talks on Ukraine war, reportedly adding Europeans to the table (16:59).

But during the meeting Putin struck a notably tough tone repeating many of his maximalist demands that are unlikely to be acceptable to Ukraine or Europe (15:24).

Separately, Ukraine’s Zelenskyy warned against “strange” attempts agree on “a new security framework between Europe and Russia,” and urged European leaders to “pay attention” to what is being proposed (13:04).

He also revealed that Starshield systems, which play a critical role for Ukraine’s army, appeared to be throttled again, disrupting its ability to defend itself from Russian attacks (10:08, 13:07).

If you have any tips, comments or suggestions, email me at jakub.krupa@theguardian.com.

I am also on Bluesky at @jakubkrupa.bsky.social and on X at @jakubkrupa.

'I think progress was made today,' Witkoff tells CNN

Speaking to CNN and Russian media on departure from Moscow, Witkoff said:

“I think progress was made today. … I think it was made earlier today. Abu Dhabi was, people didn’t think that we were going to restart trilateral. We’ve restarted it; we’ve set a new meeting now on top of that, and this is what President Trump wants to see.”

Witkoff, Kushner en route to Dublin to meet with Zelenskyy

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have left Moscow en route for Dublin where they are going to meet with Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ireland’s public broadcaster RTÉ reported.

Flightradar24 records show that they are now in fact in Helsinki, Finland and they are expected to continue the trip to Ireland shortly.

Your guess is as good as mine as to whether they are in the Finnish capital just to refuel their plane or perhaps they are catching up with Finland’s influential president Alexander Stubb, who play an important role in the peace process behind the scenes.

Kremlin welcomes useful talks with US on Ukraine, says process will be continued

The Kremlin said that talks between Russian president Vladimir Putin and two US envoys had been useful and that the American side had supported Putin’s proposal for a joint humanitarian mission to a city in eastern Ukraine, Reuters reported.

Yuri Ushakov, the Kremlin aide, said Putin would continue discussions on Ukraine with US president Donald Trump at an Apec summit in China later this month and that direct peace talks with Ukraine, which resumed this week after a pause of 9 months, would continue.

Ushakov said that Russia had made clear to the US envoys that Nato could not expand further and expressed hope that Europe would support talks on a new European security architecture.

Italy’s anti-vax medics eye return to frontline duty

Angela Giuffrida

in Rome

A controversial bill approved in October in the lower house of Italy’s parliament includes measures that allow healthcare workers who were struck off their professional registers during the pandemic for serious violations connected to their anti-vaccination beliefs – for example, promoting treatments that lacked a scientific basis – to apply to be reinstated.

The bill is being championed by the prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party and is strongly backed by its far-right coalition partner, the League.

But with allies in Forza Italia split, its approval in the lower house hinged on support from National Future (FN), a rival far-right force led by the former army general Roberto Vannacci, whose emergence is shaping the political landscape before general elections next year. Vannacci has voiced opposition to vaccine mandates, and his rhetoric frequently targets the vaccine-sceptic audience.

The measure still needs to clear the senate, with a vote scheduled in January. But its progress has alarmed medical experts, less because of the number of healthcare workers involved – it is believed to be very small – and more because of the risk of further eroding trust in vaccines.

Nearly one in two Italian adults are hesitant about vaccination, according to a report by the department of public health and paediatric sciences at the University of Turin published in the Lancet Regional Health Europe in February. The report, which sampled 50,000 adults across Italy, found the ambivalence was driven more by misinformation and lack of institutional trust than by fears over vaccine safety.

“The Europeans will join at the next meeting, which we consider to be a very important moment because they are our partners and it’s important to us that they take part.”

UK drone maker founded by Ukrainians hits £4.5bn value after raising £500m

Jasper Jolly

Meanwhile, a London-based naval drone maker founded by Ukrainians has reached a £4.5bn valuation after it raised more than £500m from investors including the UK government.

UForce, which makes military drones for land, air and sea, received £113m from the UK’s national wealth fund. The investment makes UForce one of the UK’s fastest-growing unicorns – or startups with a valuation of more than $1bn. Its drones have been used extensively in the war in Ukraine.

The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, met the UForce chief executive, Oleg Rogynskyy, on Thursday onboard the British aircraft carrier HMS Prince of Wales during a defence conference in Oslo, Norway.

The UK’s Ministry of Defence noted UForce’s maritime capabilities in particular, amid concerns over the increasing threat from Russia in the north Atlantic and North Sea. Russian naval vessels and its “shadow fleet” have been accused of sabotage and spying operations on cables and pipelines, while the UK is planning a fleet of sea-borne drones in the northern seas to track Russia’s nuclear submarine fleet.

Streeting on Thursday piloted a UForce MV7 uncrewed vessel located more than 1,500 miles away in the Atlantic Ocean near Portugal.

Former pro-Russian presidential contender Georgescu indicted on fraud charges

Meanwhiel, Romanian prosecutors said on Thursday they had indicted Călin Georgescu, the pro-Russian former frontrunner in the country’s 2024 cancelled presidential election, on charges of orchestrating a €1.1m fraud scheme.

Prosecutors said Georgescu managed an organised crime group that prompted a Romanian businessman to give them €1.1m by making him believe they could help him get a credit line of up to €15m from a foreign financial institution, Reuters reported.

Georgescu has been in pretrial detention since late September. In posts on Georgescu’s Facebook account, his wife, Cristela Georgescu, denied the charges and said they were politically motivated.

Putin's maximalist rhetoric once again suggests no plans to compromise to end war - snap analysis

Jakub Krupa

Vladimir Putin’s comments during his meeting with the two US envoys make it clear that getting a deal with Russia will not be easy.

During his talks with Witkoff and Kushner, the Russian president doubled down on his demand to retain the Russia-occupied Ukrainian territoryand opposed any foreign peacekeeping troops in the country – a key part of Europe’s planned security guarantees for Kyiv.

Instead, he continues to push for broader talks on rolling back Europe’s post-1997 Nato security architecture, a move which Zelenskyy called “strange” and urged Europe to watch closely.

Putin’s proposal for “a humanitarian mission” in Kostyantynivka is likely to be seen by Europeans as merely a token gesture designed to distract from his otherwise hardline stance.

As our Russia expert, Pjotr Sauer, said after yesterday’s discussions: “Russia appears to be seeking to revive demands it presented to Nato in 2021,” with maximalist conditions on future enlargement and deployments.

articles.title: Ghana announces first-ever hydrocarbon discovery in carbonate reserve
articles.summary: Ghana's President John Dramani Mahama on Wednesday announced the country's first-ever hydrocarbon discovery in an offshore carbonate reserve. The well lies some 150 kilometers off Ghana's coast in water more than 2000 meters deep.
articles.preview: John Dramani Mahama Ghana has reached a new milestone in its energy sector. The country has announced the discovery of hydrocarbons off its coast, in a type of reservoir never before successfully identified within its territory. The discovery was made in the Deepwater Cape Three Points offshore block, located approximately 148 kilometers off the Ghanaian coast. The Nya Gyidie-1X exploration well revealed the presence of hydrocarbons in a carbonate geological formation—a first for the country.
articles.body:
John Dramani Mahama

Ghana has reached a new milestone in its energy sector. The country has announced the discovery of hydrocarbons off its coast, in a type of reservoir never before successfully identified within its territory.

The discovery was made in the Deepwater Cape Three Points offshore block, located approximately 148 kilometers off the Ghanaian coast. The Nya Gyidie-1X exploration well revealed the presence of hydrocarbons in a carbonate geological formation—a first for the country.

According to President John Dramani Mahama, this breakthrough opens up new prospects for oil and gas exploration in Ghana. Until now, the country’s commercial discoveries had primarily been found in sandstone reservoirs.

Located in waters more than 2,200 metres deep, the well has not yet yielded information on the type or size of the resource. Further analysis is underway to gauge the full extent of the potential.

Ghanaian authorities hope that this development will attract new investment and bolster national energy production. The government is particularly focused on revitalising offshore exploration and replenishing its hydrocarbon reserves.

Israel denounced the move as “completely unacceptable” on Wednesday after prominent Israeli settler Yossi Dagan said French authorities turned him back last week when he flew into a Paris airport.

Dagan, who is a member of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, was “subject to an administrative ban from the territory due to his active role in implementing the settlement policy in the West Bank” according to his office.

“Settlement building is contrary to international law and undermines the two-state solution,” the French ministry said.

According to the ministry, Dagan was “pulled aside and questioned” at the airport’s passport control before being informed that he was banned from entering French territory “due to his active role in implementing the settlement policy in the West Bank.”

Dagan said Wednesday that he was undeterred by the ban and was proud to “build the historic homeland of the Jewish people”, while Israeli’s foreign ministry said the measures against Dagan were based on “political and ideological grounds”.

“Israel will demand an explanation from the French government and consider its next steps accordingly,” it added.

Increasing friction

The incident comes amid growing tension between Israel and European countries around illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank, which have proliferated under Netanyahu’s government.

France, along with 11 other countries, announced its intention to restrict trade with illegal settlements in the Palestinian territory in September, which spurred outrage from Israeli officials.

On Monday, a French parliamentary committee approved a bill banning the imports of settlement goods and services contributing to settlement construction, with further discussion scheduled for November 19.

There are at least 148 illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank and 15 in occupied East Jerusalem, now home to about 750,000 Israelis, according to Israeli anti-settlement watchdog Peace Now.

Earlier this year, France banned far-right Israeli ministers, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who are both members of Netanyahu’s cabinet.

articles.title: What have the talks with Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi achieved for Ukraine?
articles.summary: The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months have ended with an agreement on exchanging prisoners. Does this mark a genuine breakthrough and a step toward peace?

articles.body:
What do the talks in Abu Dhabi mean for Ukraine?

November 12, 2026

The first trilateral talks between Ukraine, the US and Russia in nine months have ended with an agreement on exchanging prisoners. Does this mark a genuine breakthrough and a step toward peace?

The two-day talks between delegations from Ukraine, the US and Russia in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11 ended without a ceasefire agreement.

The main outcome was an agreement on a prisoner exchange.

"We have agreed on the largest humanitarian release of prisoners, and tomorrow we will finalize the numbers," Jared Kushner announced after the talks. US envoys Kushner and Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow on Thursday, where they are due to meet President Vladimir Putin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had earlier suggested an exchange of "1,000 for 1,000" prisoners, or "1,500 for 1,500." Russia said a large-scale prisoner exchange with Ukraine could take place within the next two to three weeks.

Following the meetings, Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that the parties had discussed security guarantees and that "the first step should be ending this war and ensuring Ukraine's security." He also stressed that Europe should be involved "at every stage of genuine diplomacy."

How significant is the prisoner swap?

Experts interviewed by DW agree that the main outcome of the talks is humanitarian.

"The agreement on a prisoner exchange is already a major step forward," says Artjom Bronzhukov of the Ukrainian think tank Polityka.

Pavlo Lakiychuk of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies Strategy XXI also viewed it as a "very tangible result." He told DW that "getting our people back is already a major success. That is why it is worth continuing."

A real breakthrough, he added, would be the release of civilian detainees from territories occupied since 2014, particularly people from Crimea, who have been held in Russian prisons for years.

Empty diplomacy without a real breakthrough?

Davyd Arakhamia, head of the ruling Servant of the People parliamentary faction and Ukraine's representative at the talks in Abu Dhabi, gave a positive assessment of the trilateral talks with the US and Russia, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached by the end of the year.

"I think the Russians came with extremely strict instructions, and it was difficult to ease the tone of the discussion. But the way the US representatives structured the talks with a view to the postwar situation in both countries opened up a dialogue, in my opinion, and allowed us to work together more productively," Arakhamia said at a joint press conference with US and Ukrainian representatives following the talks.

Iuliia Osmolovska of the Kyiv office of the international think tank GLOBSEC cautions against reading too much into the positive assessments of the talks from Washington and Kyiv.

"Diplomats taking part in negotiations will never say that everything went badly and that they have no expectations. Even when no results are achieved, they will still emphasize that the talks were constructive," she said. "For anyone familiar with diplomatic language, these are simply standard phrases."

Experts: chances for Russia-Ukraine ceasefire low as things currently stand

Osmolovska points to a joint assessment by 71 Ukrainian security and defense experts published by GLOBSEC in the summer. According to the assessment, the chances of a peace agreement or at least a ceasefire being reached this year or next stand at just 19%.

She blames this on the fact that neither side is "ready" for genuine negotiations. Russia, in particular, has yet to accept that its objectives cannot be achieved by military means. "What we are seeing now is more of a farce, an attempt by all sides to put a brave face on things and create the impression that something is moving forward," Osmolovska said.

Artjom Bronzhukov sees the talks as a way for Moscow to buy time.

"The visits by the Russian delegation, particularly under the leadership of Vladimir Medinsky, are nothing more than an attempt to stall and sell empty promises to the US administration in the form of grand agreements, in order to continue receiving so-called gestures of goodwill from Washington, such as the lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel," the political scientist says.

Redrawing borders to make Putin feel like a winner?

Ahead of the talks, several Western media outlets reported on new US proposals concerning disputed territories. The Economist, for example, reported on a proposal to redraw the administrative boundaries of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions. However, a member of the Ukrainian delegation stressed that there had "never been any discussion of concessions on territories occupied by Russia."

Washington made no official comment on the reports.

Kyrylo Budanov, a member of the negotiating delegation and head of the Ukrainian president's office, declined to say whether Russia had used the talks to demand that Ukrainian troops withdraw from the Donbas. Asked by journalists whether Moscow was still insisting that Ukraine pull out of the region, Budanov said the content of the negotiations would remain confidential until an agreement was reached.

"The issues discussed in the talks are matters for negotiation. The only thing that matters is the outcome. Once we achieve it, it will be made public," Budanov said.

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, took a different tone, declaring that "every inch of our land will be returned to Russia one way or another." He was responding to reports in European media that Ukraine was rejecting territorial concessions.

Putin demands large swaths of Ukrainian territory

In addition to the Crimean Peninsula, annexed in 2014, Russian President Vladimir Putin claims the four Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson in their entirety as Russian territory, even though Russia does not have full military control over them.

"Putin is not fighting over villages and ruined cowsheds in the Donbas. He is fighting for geopolitical influence and trying to exploit the collapse of the old world order," says Artjom Bronzhukov.

The expert from the Polityka think tank recalls that Ukraine was already asked in early 2026 to withdraw its troops from the part of the Donbas it controls and turn the area into a free economic zone. Such a zone "would very quickly become a Russian-controlled area," he warns.

Pavlo Lakiychuk questions the idea of changing administrative boundaries.

"Why would Putin stop there?" asks the expert from the Strategy XXI center. In his view, US negotiators are seeking to extract unilateral concessions from Ukraine "step by step" without demanding anything in return from Russia.

Iuliia Osmolovska describes the proposal as "very original," but says it would pose risks for Ukraine's leadership. Even if the Ukrainian delegation agreed to it, which Osmolovska doubts, the decision would have to be explained to the public, which, she says, is not ready to accept it.

The GLOBSEC expert points out that, following the last harsh winter, marked by shortages of electricity and heating, only 5% of Ukrainians were willing to make concessions to Russia in exchange for an end to attacks on the energy sector.

What next after Abu Dhabi?

Following the meeting between Jared Kushner, US special envoy Steve Witkoff and Vladimir Putin in Moscow, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said he wants to "coordinate positions with the Americans once again." No further trilateral meetings have been announced so far.

Iuliia Osmolovska believes the parties will sooner or later have to admit that the negotiations have reached a dead end. She expects each side to return to military action.

Pavlo Lakiychuk, by contrast, believes the talks should continue, if only to secure the return of prisoners. He is also convinced that Europeans "will always be there," because the issue is not just the Russian-Ukrainian war but the security of the entire continent.

articles.body:
The planet is “not dying, it is being killed and we know by who”, said Greta Thunberg, who excoriated world governments for their failure to prevent environmental breakdown in her first appearance at the annual UN climate talks in five years.

Thunberg, 23, the Swedish activist who became famous for heading the school climate strike movement, delivered her stark message to those gathered at the Cop31 summit in Antalya, Turkey, amid the ongoing failure by countries to adequately address the climate crisis.

“It [Earth] is being killed by the very same people thought to come to our rescue,” Thunberg said.

“No one is coming to our rescue. When our human rights are being threatened by states and other institutions, it’s our duty to stand up and be the adult in the room and fight for everyone’s human rights.”

Thunberg, who in recent years has shifted her focus towards other areas such as the conflict in Gaza, linked worsening global heating to other calamities such as war in an appearance alongside activists from Nepal, Canada and Australia.

“We are heading towards a future of more genocides and more ecocides and the complete compromise of our basic rights and where basic necessities become luxuries,” she said.

“It’s more clear than ever in spaces like these that the situation could not be any less under control. The planet is not dying, it is being killed.”

The intervention, on the fourth day of the two-week summit, came as world leaders who travelled to the Mediterranean coastal city delivered their own verdicts on the climate crisis and the faltering progress to address it.

Andy Burnham, the British prime minister, who was the only G7 leader to attend the talks, said in a speech that the record hot summer in the UK was “not normal”.

“The climate crisis is not a distant threat; it is upon us all now, devastating lives and livelihoods everywhere,” said Burnham, who promised the UK would get to net zero emissions, and backed a proposal for countries to further electrify their economies.

Beth John, a climate justice adviser at Oxfam GB, said Burnham’s appearance “sends a positive signal”. But she added: “Showing up is not enough: a crisis of this scale needs substantive action, not just signals. The real test of climate leadership is delivery, not declarations.”

The electrification goal is one of the main potential promises expected at the talks, which are being jointly presided over by Turkey and Australia. Some countries want the agreement text to specify that the electricity will be derived from clean energy sources.

Campaigners have criticised governments for their slow pace of emissions cuts and for, so far, failing to rally around a phaseout of fossil fuels in the negotiations.

Current policies are set to heat the planet by 2.7C by the end of the century, a report by Climate Action Tracker found on Thursday. The catastrophic rise in temperatures is slightly more than the group expected last year and well above the 1.5C that world leaders have promised.

Thursday was rife with accounts of the harm caused by the climate crisis. Gita Chaudhary, Nepal’s environment minister, recounted the disastrous landslide – caused by a melting glacier – that struck the country in August, claiming more than 1,500 lives.

“We call the catastrophic climate change event we suffered a mountain tsunami,” Chaudhary told the Guardian. “We lost people, we lost lives, we lost property. Nepal is working for rehabilitation, reconstruction and rebuilding the infrastructure. But the communities, the culture, the lives, we cannot revive.”

In the main conference room, a speech by Mohammad Mustafa, the prime minister of Palestine, drew a standing ovation from delegates as he described the environmental impact of the three-year war with Israel.

“Israel’s restrictions on access to land, water and natural resources have compounded Palestine’s climate challenges,” said Mustafa, who spelled out how widespread destruction in Gaza, including to water supplies, sewerage and farmland, had worsened environmental and health risks.

The Turkish hosts of Cop31 have repeatedly accused Israel of genocide and refused to invite the country’s leadership to Antalya. Israel denies that it has committed genocide and insists it has fought a legitimate war to safeguard its own security.

Another country not formally present at the talks is the US, which did not send a delegation. Donald Trump has withdrawn the country from the international climate framework, derided climate science as a “hoax”, and claimed he would not permit any new wind turbines.

This stance earned a rebuke from John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, who has made the trip to Turkey along with 20 Democratic members of Congress and two state governors. “He’s the biggest loser we’ve seen in a long time on all of these issues,” Kerry said of Trump in response to a question from the Guardian.

The crushing midterm election win by the Democrats has raised hopes here at Cop of the US re-engaging on the climate crisis. But Gavin Newsom, the governor of California, warned the final two years of the Trump presidency would not see fundamental change on climate policy.

“I don’t want to romanticise what this will mean,” Newsom said on Thursday. “I don’t expect they’ll do anything but double down.”

articles.preview: Government proposal aims to reduce number of children in custody in England and Wales and boost youth employment Children found guilty of robbery, dealing drugs to other children or violent disorder will no longer have to disclose their criminal records to prospective employers under sweeping government proposals to change the youth justice system.
articles.body:
Children found guilty of robbery, dealing drugs to other children or violent disorder will no longer have to disclose their criminal records to prospective employers under sweeping government proposals to change the youth justice system.

People in England and Wales will not have to share records of crimes committed when they were under 18 for the rest of their lives under the proposals, which ministers say will boost youth employment and make life fairer for people from disadvantaged backgrounds in particular.

The proposals, which are subject to consultation, are part of a wider set of changes that aim to sharply reduce the number of children in custody and increase support for those who are convicted of crimes.

Jake Richards, a justice minister, told the Guardian: “Where it’s safe, we believe as a government, people should have second chances – second chances to make something of themselves, to contribute to work and to turn their back on crime.

“The system at the moment doesn’t discern for offences committed when you were a child [and] those committed as an adult.”

Ministers have been talking about reducing the number of people who have to disclose childhood convictions for several years. David Lammy, the former justice secretary, found in a 2017 review that criminal records from childhood were one reason black and minority people faced discrimination later in life.

Richards plans to reduce the number of offences that would require lifelong disclosure on standard and enhanced DBS checks by the person who committed them.

If the proposals become law, people convicted of violent disorder, supplying drugs to a child, robbery, affray and actual bodily harm when under 18 would no longer automatically have to disclose those offences for the rest of their lives.

If they are convicted of one of those offences but do not get a custodial sentence, they will have to disclose the offence for five and a half years. If they receive a sentence of two years or less, they would have to disclose it for 11 years.

Anyone given a longer custodial sentence would still have a lifetime obligation to tell prospective employers.

If someone is convicted of a crime that results in a fine, they will no longer have to disclose it, as opposed to for the next six months as the law currently stipulates.

Positions in the UK that require a standard or enhanced DBS check include teaching and early years work, social work, healthcare and transport jobs such as taxi driving.

Other changes include ending the automatic disclosure of any out-of-court resolution and ending a rule that lengthens how long it takes for a conviction to become spent if the person is convicted of a second crime during their rehabilitation period.

Campaigners welcomed the proposed changes, saying they will boost youth employment. Companies said criminal convictions are the second biggest barrier to employing people from disadvantaged backgrounds.

Paula Harriott, the chief executive of the charity Unlock, said: “It is not proportionate or fair that each year tens of thousands of people have to disclose childhood offences that are irrelevant to who they are today.

“Given the long shadow a criminal record casts, and the barriers to employment, education and volunteering it creates, it is right that the government is consulting on these reforms.”

Former offenders have also given backing to the plans. Speaking to reporters after a launch event in London, Joanne [not her real name], a 22-year-old who spent 18 months in a young offender institution as a child, said the reforms would have changed her life had they been in place earlier.

“If my criminal record from five and a half years ago was gone now, I would be able to achieve my dreams, literally, and achieve everything I want to do, which is own my own residential care facility with staff that employs people with lived experience,” she said.

Joanne said she had been convicted of several counts of affray and assault – the first when she was 10 years old – after being exploited by a gang who pushed her to sell drugs. “If I was on the street and I had some drugs and somebody came over to me trying to take it off me, I would have to then use violence so they don’t take that from me,” she said.

“Because if that was to happen, and it was taken off me, the punishment would then come to me, and I would be hurt.”

articles.body:
South Africa

Days after a drubbing at the ballot box, the leaders of South Africa's ruling African National Congress met to discuss the way forward. The party has vowed to enter a period of "soul-searching" to see how to win back voters. But to remain in local government, it will have to engage with other parties.

African National Congress national spokesperson Mahlengi Bhengu-Motsiri said that President Cyril Ramaphosa will not resign, as the party's top leadership met on Thursday at the special National Executive Committee meeting to discuss the way forward following recent local government elections.

The party’s vote share dropped 15 percentage points to just 31 percent.

"There is a lot of fabrication about the President, that he has offered to resign, we urge South Africans to treat that as such. The ANC performance, this local government elections requires a proper reflection today. This is the day when that is going to happen," she said.

While speaking about how ANC will engage with other political parties in forming coalition governments in municipalities where no party secured an outright majority, Bhengu-Motsiri stated that the party respects the choice of the voters.

"This NEC will receive reports on the initial engagements with other political parties and consider the mandating guide for adoption. The guide will then set out the mandate for the ANC’s appointed negotiations team," she added.

The ANC, which once commanded 70 percent of the vote and had no challengers, conceded to being humbled in the local elections — its worst performance at the ballot box ever.

The party's secretary-general called it a “catastrophic outcome” for the ANC and said it would enter a period of soul-searching to see how it could win back the trust of South Africa's people.

Two years ago, the ANC lost its parliamentary majority in a national election with 40 percent of the vote. It considered that a disaster, and a chance for self-reflection, but its supporters have continued to desert it.

The ANC has often pointed to the difficulties in reversing nearly a half-century of racist laws under apartheid and hundreds of years of European colonialism before that.

But the most pressing problems for many South Africans in 2026 boil down to a failure of basic government services, with communities across the nation faced with a lack of electricity in their neighborhoods, broken or nonexistent water and sewage systems, garbage piling up on streets and a shortage of housing that leaves millions living in shacks.

The Istanbul Governor’s Office sealed the office of Lambda Istanbul LGBTI+ Solidarity Association on Wednesday, as a crackdown continues across the country targeting LGBTQ+ groups. In a statement, Lambda Istanbul said the move was a further attempt to "isolate LGBTI+ individuals, deprive them of their living spaces, and restrict their freedom to organise". Lambda Istanbul was founded in 1993 out of an attempt by LGBTQ+ activists to stage the city's first Pride parade. Its office was opened in 2002 and it was formally registered as an association in 2006. "We do not accept the attempt to frame our association’s activities – which we have conducted openly, transparently, and in compliance with official records for years – as the 'operation of an unauthorised social club', nor do we accept the encroachment upon our living spaces!" the group said in its statement. Another organisation, Hevi LGBTI+, also announced on Thursday that their termination had been requested in an indictment prepared by the Istanbul Chief Public Prosecutor's Office. The group also said the indictment was seeking to prosecute five founding members of Hevi over violation of the law on associations. Crackdown continues Homosexuality is not illegal in Turkey, and social attitudes vary, but the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) has increasingly targeted the LGBTQ+ community in recent years. President Recep Tayyip Erdogan announced earlier this year that 2026 onwards would be the "Decade of the Family" and has characterised the LGBTQ+ community as a threat to family values. Hundreds of people and organisations have been detained and raided in recent months as part of the "My Family is Safe" operation, while hundreds of social media accounts and websites have been banned. Detainees have faced charges of "obscenity", "assisting prostitution" and having "financial links abroad", while the government and its supporters have pushed a narrative of protecting family values. At the request of the Turkish authorities, X has blocked the accounts of Amnesty International Turkey, the left-wing Evrensel newspaper, Academics for Peace, and the Media and Law Studies Association, among others. Other accounts blocked include the Sexual Education, Treatment and Research Association (Cetad), which provides support to people living with HIV and Aids, and the Psychiatric Association of Turkey (TPD). Another major target was Kaos GL, one of Turkey's most prominent LGBTQ+ organisations, which the Ankara chief prosecutor's office said had been subject to 21 arrests as part of an investigation. articles.body:
November 12, 2026

The Sri Lankan government is looking to replace a controversial anti-terror law but critics say the new one is just as bad.

For 46-year-old Ganesan (name changed) from Batticaloa in eastern Sri Lanka, any discussion of terrorism brings back memories of his two-year-old daughter, who was killed in the 2019 Easter Sunday attacks. She was one of 270 people who lost their lives in a series of coordinated bombings targeting three churches and three luxury hotels across the island nation.

The attacks were the deadliest in Sri Lanka since the end of its civil war in 2009. Over 500 people were injured.

Ganesan's daughter was killed in an attack on the Zion Church in Batticaloa.

But Ganesan remains skeptical when asked about the new counterterrorism bill pushed by the government in Sri Lanka.

"Laws against terrorism are necessary to prevent terrorist attacks, but they should not target the innocent or suppress human rights," he told DW.

The administration led by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake and his National People's Power faction

has proposed the Protection of the State from Terrorism Act (PSTA) as a replacement for the existing Prevention of Terrorism Act (PTA). The PTA has many critics who claim that the contentious law has enabled arbitrary detention and the torture of detainees for decades.

The government argues that a robust anti-terrorism law is needed to address the increasingly complex local and international activities of extremist groups.

What do rights groups say about the new bill?

But rights groups are now also sharply criticizing the new bill. Activist argue that the changes will not bring about any improvement, warning that the draft features an overly broad definition of terrorism, provides inadequate judicial oversight, and grants extensive powers to law enforcement authorities. Activists also warn that the proposed law has only limited safeguards against official abuse.

The bill, for instance, allows security forces to stop, search and question individuals on the basis of "reasonable suspicion," enter and search premises, and seize items on suspicion of them being linked to an offense under the terrorism act.

"The definition of the term 'terrorism' in the bill as presently drafted is highly problematic. The term is unclear, and its meaning has not been clearly defined," Visakesa Chandrasekaram, a film director and human rights lawyer, told DW.

"Such lack of clarity in the law may result in violations of the fundamental rights of the people," he added.

Chandrasekaram also pointed out that the bill would confer police powers on the military, which is neither trained to investigate criminal offenses nor equipped to protect the rights of people targeted in such investigations.

This, he warned, could lead to the "militarization" of the law enforcement process.

Is the new law just PTA all over again?

Dhanushka Silva, a lawyer, said the proposed law is not much different from the existing one.

"The present government pledged to repeal the PTA in their 2024 election manifesto. But now the government seems to replace it with a new act that is a replica of the PTA," he told DW.

Silva believes the new bill, PSTA, could be misused to suppress democratic freedoms and muzzle dissent and free speech.

Under Section 9 of the PSTA, even posts or statements made on social media could be subject to scrutiny due to the broad definition of terrorism-related offenses in the bill, he explained.

The section further suggests that individuals who share content deemed to be a terrorism offense could face up to 15 years of rigorous imprisonment, according to the the lawyer.

"This is a big blow to freedom of speech in a democratic society like ours," he said.

The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) has also called on the government to ensure that the bill is consistent with international human rights law.

It noted that the PSTA, despite containing some additional safeguards and improvements on previous drafts, reproduces a number of shortcomings in the PTA and other, older counter-terrorism bills.

The legislation "should include robust safeguards against torture, ill-treatment, enforced disappearance and coercive interrogation," it said in a statement.

Government spokesperson Nalinda Jayatissa, however, rejected the allegations by rights activists and insisted that the new law would not compromise civil liberties and press freedom.

Calls for Colombo to uphold human rights commitments

Passing the new counterterrorism legislation could also have economic and foreign policy ramifications for Sri Lanka.

The United Nations, which has repeatedly urged Colombo to repeal the PTA, has called for further revisions to the proposed PSTA.

The European Union has likewise urged Sri Lanka to uphold its international human rights obligations if it wishes to continue benefiting from the bloc's Generalized Scheme of Preferences Plus (GSP+), which grants preferential access to the EU market to eligible developing countries.

Failure to meet these requirements could result in the suspension of GSP+ preferences, likely to trigger significant economic penalties for the country.

During a parliamentary debate on November 12, Speaker Jagath Wickramaratne said that some provisions of the proposed law were inconsistent with the constitution.

The legislation was also challenged before the Supreme Court, which outlined several amendments and said Parliament could pass the measure once the changes were made.

Parliament has yet to set a date for a vote.

articles.title: UK court convicts 2 Iranian men of spying on journalists
articles.summary: A London court has found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling reporters for a Persian-language television station critical of Iran's government. One was also convicted of planning a violent attack against them.
articles.preview: UK convicts 2 Iranian men of spying on Persian language journalists November 12, 2026 A London court has found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling reporters for a Persian-language television station critical of Iran's government. One was also convicted of planning a violent attack against them. Two Iranian men were found guilty of spying on dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Thursday.
articles.body:
UK convicts 2 Iranian men of spying on Persian language journalists

November 12, 2026

A London court has found two Iranian citizens guilty of surveilling reporters for a Persian-language television station critical of Iran's government. One was also convicted of planning a violent attack against them.

Two Iranian men were found guilty of spying on dissident journalists in Britain on behalf of Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Thursday.

British counterterrorism police said the case reflected intensifying hostile Iranian activity in the country, an issue that recently made headlines amid the security scare at the RAF Fairford airbase that's a major operational site in Europe for the US Air Force.

The men, both in their 40s, were arrested last year, with Iran repeatedly rejecting the allegations against them.

What did the court rule?

The Woolwich Crown Court in London convicted one of the Iranian citizens not just of spying on journalists working for the Persian-language dissident TV channel Iran International, but of plotting a violent attack against one or more of them.

The second individual had also faced charges of plotting an attack but was only convicted of spying on the reporters.

One of the convicted defendants said he was acting under duress after his family was threatened, and the other said he did not know that his actions were assisting Iranian intelligence.

A third defendant, a 57-year-old Iranian man, was acquitted of all charges.

The men were accused of engaging in conduct likely to assist the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), Iran's multi-discipline military force that's seen as closer to the country's religious leadership and more influential than its regular armed forces.

The UK formally designated the IRGC as a threat to national security in July, meaning that supporting or assisting the organization can carry penalties of up to 14 years in prison as part of new rules on national security and state threats.

Sentencing in this case is still pending and is scheduled for mid-December.

"This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime," said Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service's special crime and counter-terrorism division.

The two men were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos, and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online

"Thankfully, the defendants were stopped before any attack could take place," prosecutor Ferguson said.

Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing Vicki Evans said that the IRGC or "middlemen" for Iranian intelligence were directing the plot.

Iran's government had repeatedly denied the allegations, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi saying he was "disturbed" by the trio's arrests last May.

Not the first plot targeting Iran International

There have been four cases targeting the Persian language television channel Iran International since late 2023.

In July, two Romanian men were jailed for stabbing a journalist outside his home in 2024.

A spokesman for the broadcaster's parent company, Volant Media, said in a statement that Thursday's verdicts "don't make the lives of our journalists any safer so long as the Islamic Republic of Iran continues its campaign of death threats and violence against them."

Iran International reported that a British barrister was also one of the targets.

What other alleged signs of Iranian hostile activity in the UK are there?

British law enforcement has been warning of an uptick of hostile Iranian activity in recent years, particularly since the US military operations against Tehran began earlier this year.

Most notably, the UK has accused Iran of being behind a suspected plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in September, after which US President Donald Trump withdrew some long-range bombers from the site.

Three men were indicted in the US in relation to that plot this week, while two others currently face charges in the UK.

But beyond this, the head of Britain's MI5 domestic intelligence agency Ken MacCullum said in October that Iran-linked operations had led to more than 50 arrests in the last year. He also said known cases of so-called state threats had more than quadrupled in a decade.

Counter-terrorism police chief Evans said she expected this trend to continue.

France this week also accused Iran of being behind a cyberattack targeting refrigeration units at hundreds of supermarkets in October, although Iran denied any involvement.

European governments are on heightened alert for so-called hybrid warfare tactics, from Russia as well as Iran, amid the geopolitical tensions of recent years. New technologies like low-cost drones and AI are also threatening to make such activities cheaper, harder to trace, and potentially more effective.

articles.body:
A senior leader of Colombia's largest criminal gang, the Gulf Clan, is among eight people killed in an air strike carried out by the country's armed forces, according to President Abelardo de la Espriella.

De la Espriella said he had personally authorised the bombing targeting the Gulf Clan in the province of Antioquia, in north-west Colombia.

He added that Haminton Mosquera, whom he described as a senior member of the crime gang and one of 10 "priority targets" for Colombia's security forces, had been "brought down".

De la Espriella was elected in June after campaigning on a promise to crack down on Colombia's powerful criminal gangs, including by launching air strikes.

In a post on X, external, he said that Mosquera was suspected of having ordered attacks against the security forces, including the murder of a police officer in the municipality of Tarazá last year.

The Gulf Clan has been engaging in criminal activities for decades, mainly trafficking cocaine from Colombia to destinations in the US and Europe but also illegal mining and people smuggling.

The US added it to its list of Foreign Terrorist Organisations (FTOs) last year.

In his post, President de la Espriella said that "the offensive won't stop" and vowed to regain control of areas currently controlled by criminal organisations such as the Gulf Clan.

While his offensive against criminal gangs has been welcomed by many living in areas where extortion and gang violence are rampant, de la Espriella has faced criticism for the way he has made some of his announcements on security.

Less than a month after taking office, he published a video showing him walking among 23 body bags containing the remains of 23 people killed in an air strike on a suspected guerrilla camp.

On Wednesday, he shared a photo, external in which he can be seen writing his campaign slogan, "Welcome to the miracle homeland" on a bomb.

He has also defended his decision to wear an army uniform at a recent event in Cúcuta at which he confronted a detainee suspected of being a Farc rebel.

"What did you make of the bomb I sent you, signed by me?," the president can be heard asking the man.

He later told journalists that he wore the uniform because "I am a soldier of the homeland. That's why I dress like a soldier, because I came to serve Colombia. Because I honour the heroes, police officers and military."

articles.body:
Un gruppo di liceali francesi va in gita scolastica a Napoli per scoprire le rovine di Pompei e i corpi pietrificati dall’eruzione del Vesuvio. Come colti da una vertigine, uno dopo l’altro si lasciano sopraffare dal desiderio e dalla rabbia. Al suo primo lungometraggio come regista, la direttrice della fotografia Marine Atlan cerca di catturare l’essenza del cinema d’autore francese contemporaneo. Da una parte la naturalezza, l’esuberanza giovanile e il luccichio incantatore della superficie. Dall’altro la gravità, il peso delle origini e la ricerca di una profondità mitologica.

Raphaël Nieuwjaer, Cahiers du Cinéma

Francia / Italia 2026, 145’. In sala

Giappone 2026, 100’. In sala

Fujino è molto popolare per i manga che disegna per il giornale della scuola. Lo stesso giornale comincia a pubblicare anche i manga di Kyomono, un’altra studente che soffre d’ansia e non esce mai di casa. Quando le due ragazze s’incontrano diventano amiche per la pelle e cominciano a collaborare, arrivando giovanissime al successo. Poi però Kyomono s’iscrive all’accademia di belle arti. La rottura tra loro è dolorosa, ma quello che segue è straziante. Nel suo secondo film del 2026, tratto dall’omonimo manga di Tatsuki Fujimoto, Kore-eda riflette sull’angosciante rimpianto che si può provare pensando a come sarebbero potute andare diversamente le cose. Guardare indietro è un gesto autentico e vitale, ma al di fuori del regno dell’arte è struggente e futile. Non si può cambiare nulla guardando indietro; è semplicemente un luogo per la tristezza e il rimpianto. La dinamica emotiva di questo film è coinvolgente, un’opera di grande chiarezza, intimità e profondità.

Peter Bradshaw, The Guardian

Spagna / Francia 2026, 102’. In sala

Esteban è un regista acclamato e con un passato turbolento che si ricongiunge alla figlia, un’attrice in difficoltà con cui ha un rapporto teso e a cui offre il ruolo da protagonista nel suo nuovo film. La vicinanza li costringe a confrontarsi con il passato e con il dolore che affligge il loro rapporto. Nessuno dei due sembra in grado di affrontare la situazione in modo diretto e lucido. Sorogoyen conferma il suo talento raccontando una storia intima e apparentemente piccola in modo grandioso: elegante, sottile, misurato, ma senza dubbio grandioso.

Jesús Usero, AcciónCine

Questo documentario è ambientato in gran parte nei Vosgi, dove l’autore è cresciuto. Il canto della foresta è soprattutto una storia di trasmissione del sapere. Il regista ha al suo fianco il padre Michel – fotografo e naturalista, che conosce bene quell’ecosistema – e il figlio Simon. Michel condivide con loro il suo sapere, le sue esperienze e la sua filosofia di vita. Il film non si concentra sulla didattica ma conduce alla poesia, cattura la bellezza senza cercare spettacolo, anche se non manca qualche sorpresa.

Boris Bastide, Le Monde

Corea del Sud / Stati Uniti 2026, 164’. Su Netflix

Il nuovo film di Lee Chang-dong è un’avvincente e a tratti amara analisi delle divisioni di classe, delle tensioni coniugali e dei desideri latenti. Come nella commedia nera No other choice, del connazionale Park Chan-wook, lo spunto è il cinico sfruttamento aziendale. Quando Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu) perde il lavoro e la reputazione in seguito a uno sciopero violento, sua moglie Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon) stringe un inaspettato legame con Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), un’elegante documentarista che li ha avvicinati con la scusa di raccontare la loro storia. Ma le disparità socioeconomiche creano una complessa dinamica di potere; sullo sfondo aleggia la questione di chi abbia più da guadagnare da questa amicizia, insieme a una tacita tensione sessuale. Superbamente interpretato Possible love è un’opera d’intelligenza pungente e giustifica la sua generosa durata.

Wendy Ide, The Observer

articles.preview: Hardline remarks come as Ukrainian military faces disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops deployed to Ukraine, in a series of hardline remarks that came as the Ukrainian military faced renewed disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service.
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin warned US negotiators that Russia would target any foreign troops deployed to Ukraine, in a series of hardline remarks that came as the Ukrainian military faced renewed disruptions to Elon Musk’s Starlink satellite service.

During the talks at the Kremlin with the US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff on Thursday, the Russian president refused to soften his territorial demands, insisting on full control over four Ukrainian regions that Moscow claims to have annexed.

He also ruled out accepting the deployment of foreign peacekeeping troops in Ukraine, describing such a move as a “continuation of war”.

Putin’s comments appeared to severely dampen hopes that a peace deal could be within reach, after Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there was a “window of opportunity” to reach an agreement before the end of 2026.

The latest trip to Moscow by Witkoff and Kushner, who have made numerous visits to Russia, was partly aimed at securing European participation in future negotiations, according to two people familiar with the talks.

Speaking after the meeting, Witkoff confirmed that European representatives would join the next round of talks. “They’re our partners, and it’s important for them to be involved,” he told reporters as he boarded a plane leaving Moscow.

The US envoys will now travel to Dublin, Ireland, where they will meet Zelenskyy and debrief him on the Moscow meeting.

Amid a flurry of diplomatic activity, including the recent talks in Abu Dhabi, the Kremlin appears to have succeeded in reframing negotiations over the war in Ukraine as part of a broader discussion about European security.

But Europe is wary of Russian attempts to focus discussions on a European security architecture, while Moscow continues to pound Ukraine with bombs and missiles.

The EU foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, told reporters: “We already have a European security architecture in place.” Kallas pointed to the cold war-era Helsinki accords and the Budapest memorandum, which guaranteed the territorial integrity of Ukraine. “The problem is that Russia is not keeping to those agreements, so right now the focus should be that Russia actually keeps to their obligations … and they don’t attack another country again.” Focusing on a European security architecture was a “distraction” without a ceasefire, she added.

Both Washington and Moscow have been urging European leaders to appoint a single representative to lead negotiations on their behalf.

“Once a representative is appointed, a chief negotiator authorised to speak on Europe’s behalf, there will be a four-way dialogue,” Putin said on Thursday.

EU leaders are due to discuss the issue of who speaks for Europe on Friday, but so far have declined to nominate one person to speak for the bloc. One EU official said the EU would be represented by its institutions when issues concerning the union were on the table, but played down any imminent appointment. They said: “Do I expect an agreement on a special representative? My answer is no, I don’t.”

Kallas suggested she – as the EU’s high representative for foreign and security policy – should represent the EU in talks, alongside António Costa, the president of the European Council.

More than 45 European leaders are meeting in Dublin for the European Political Community summit, a gathering that brings together nearly every country on the continent, apart from the leaders of Belarus and Russia.

The French president, Emmanuel Macron, played down the importance of having a single European negotiator, saying “the content determines the format”. “There is no more US support. So there [are] some mediations, fine,” he said, referring to the process led by Kushner and Witkoff. “But at the end of the day we will be the one to define and decide for our future security as Europeans.”

The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said it was first necessary to get Putin to the negotiating table before deciding on a European envoy. Merz said: “It’s not about individuals. What matters is that Putin is prepared to hold talks.”

Meanwhile, Zelenskyy accused Musk’s Starlink satellite service of damaging Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russian drone attacks, after Ukrainian military officials reported new restrictions on the system.

According to Zelenskyy, Starshield, a military version of Starlink funded by the Pentagon, has for several days been subject to speed limits of 100mph (161km/h) along the frontline and in Russian-occupied territory.

Similar restrictions last month prompted confusion over who had ordered them, with Musk and the Trump administration pointing fingers at each other before the service was partly restored.

The latest restrictions had made it harder for Ukrainian forces to intercept Russia’s increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones, Zelenskyy said, accusing the service of “helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine”.

Kyiv has contacted Washington to seek an explanation for the disruption, which Zelenskyy said appeared to be deliberate rather than a technical fault.

articles.summary: Dutch foreign minister declines to deny talks are under way on curbing ICC powers Submitted by Sondos Asem on Thu, 11/12/2026 - 14:07 MPs asked minister if Netherlands is discussing restrictions that could shield Israeli and US officials from prosecution The Netherlands' Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen at the Nato foreign ministers' meeting in Helsingborg, Sweden on 22 May 2026 (Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP) Off Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has declined to rule out the suggestion that discussions are taking place over sweeping restrictions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), following a report that the Netherlands is negotiating with Washington over changes that could severely undermine the court's powers. Questioned in parliament on Wednesday, Berendsen said diplomatic discussions were taking place but he would not specify whether proposals to shield national leaders and restrict the court's jurisdiction were under consideration. The exchange followed a report by Dutch rights organisation The Rights Forum , citing anonymous diplomatic sources in New York, that the Netherlands was negotiating restrictions in response to US sanctions. Hanneke van der Werf MP, from the Democrats 66 party, asked whether discussions included immunity for heads of state and government, excluding nationals of countries outside the court's founding treaty from its jurisdiction, and weakening its ability to intervene when national authorities fail to prosecute. Berendsen's answers did not confirm the reported proposals, but nor did they answer whether the government would reject them. He told parliament he would send MPs a letter next week setting out the Netherlands’ position for the upcoming Assembly of States Parties, including its diplomatic approach to addressing US sanctions against the court. "Discussions are currently taking place about the diplomatic track being pursued," Berendsen said. "I cannot anticipate which subjects are or are not on the table." He added that the Netherlands could not decide the matter alone, because more than 120 member states would potentially have to reach an agreement with the US. 'All kinds of discussions are taking place, but that does not mean that this is the position the Netherlands is taking' – Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen "So the minister is not denying that it is true," Van der Werf responded. "All kinds of discussions are taking place, but that does not mean that this is the position the Netherlands is taking," Berendsen said. ICC member states are scheduled to meet in The Hague from 30 November to 7 December, after the session was relocated from New York because US sanctions and visa restrictions threatened participation. Washington imposed sanctions on the ICC as an institution on 9 October, escalating a campaign that had already targeted most of the court's judges and prosecutors. The sanctions have been imposed since February last year, in the aftermath of the arrest warrants issued by the court for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza . In the institutional sanctions, Washington granted a six-month exemption for certain operational transactions to allow time for negotiations, with its expiry on 7 April next year. US sanctions International Criminal Court hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize court from conducting transactions in US dollars, effectively cutting it off from large parts of the international financial system and potentially crippling its operations. Banks tend to over-comply with sanctions because of their dependence on that system. Any agreement to rewrite the court's core powers would face substantial legal hurdles. Under the Rome Statute’s general amendment procedure, adoption requires consensus or a two-thirds majority, followed by ratification by seven-eighths of member states before entry into force. The reported discussions echo demands previously reported by Middle East Eye. In December 2025, MEE revealed that Washington had pressed for an end to the Palestine and Afghanistan investigations and treaty changes preventing prosecutions of nationals of non-member countries, in return for lifting sanctions. Three diplomats familiar with the matter said an EU diplomat had presented the US demands to representatives of ICC member states ahead of the annual gathering of the Assembly of States Parties. The assembly ultimately reaffirmed the treaty’s integrity. One diplomat warned that amendments intended to appease Washington could damage the court more than sanctions themselves. Restrictions on prosecutions The Rights Forum reported three potential restrictions that would fundamentally alter the court’s ability to prosecute international crimes. The first would grant immunity to heads of state and government. The second would exclude nationals of non-member countries from the court’s jurisdiction, even for crimes committed on the territory of a member state. That would threaten the legal basis for prosecutions of Israeli officials over crimes in occupied Palestine. Israel has not joined the Rome Statute, but Palestine has, allowing the court to exercise territorial jurisdiction. The third reported restriction concerns complementarity: the principle under which the ICC acts when national authorities fail to genuinely investigate or prosecute. According to The Rights Forum, the proposed change could allow the existence of domestic legislation criminalising relevant conduct to block ICC proceedings, even without genuine national investigations. In its response to the organisation, the Dutch foreign ministry said no concrete proposals were currently before the Assembly of States Parties, the court’s governing body. Rights groups and legal experts have repeatedly urged the EU to activate its Blocking Statute , a legal mechanism which aims to protect EU companies and individuals from the effects of extraterritorial sanctions imposed by third countries. If activated, the statute would reassure EU-based service providers that their transactions with the ICC are protected. It essentially prohibits them from complying with foreign laws that could harm their business operations within the EU. Dutch and European leaders have pledged support but remain cautious about invoking the mechanism. Prime Minister Rob Jetten promised last month to protect the court “brick by brick”, while Berendsen has described the Blocking Statute as a drastic measure that could be used only once. EU leaders subsequently called for measures to help European companies continue serving the court. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on 20 October that activating the statute remained an option, but required careful preparation. She also urged companies against over-compliance with US restrictions during the six-month transition period. Established in 2002, the ICC is the world’s only permanent international criminal court with the mandate to investigate and prosecute individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. The court currently has over a dozen active investigations , including the situations in Darfur, Libya , Myanmar and Ukraine . Dutch foreign minister declines to deny talks are under way on curbing ICC powers Submitted by Sondos Asem on Thu, 11/12/2026 - 14:07 MPs asked minister if Netherlands is discussing restrictions that could shield Israeli and US officials from prosecution The Netherlands' Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen at the Nato foreign ministers' meeting in Helsingborg, Sweden on 22 May 2026 (Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP) Off Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen has declined to rule out the suggestion that discussions are taking place over sweeping restrictions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), following a report that the Netherlands is negotiating with Washington over changes that could severely undermine the court's powers.

Questioned in parliament on Wednesday, Berendsen said diplomatic discussions were taking place but he would not specify whether proposals to shield national leaders and restrict the court's jurisdiction were under consideration. The exchange followed a report by Dutch rights organisation The Rights Forum , citing anonymous diplomatic sources in New York, that the Netherlands was negotiating restrictions in response to US sanctions.

Hanneke van der Werf MP, from the Democrats 66 party, asked whether discussions included immunity for heads of state and government, excluding nationals of countries outside the court's founding treaty from its jurisdiction, and weakening its ability to intervene when national authorities fail to prosecute. Berendsen's answers did not confirm the reported proposals, but nor did they answer whether the government would reject them.

He told parliament he would send MPs a letter next week setting out the Netherlands’ position for the upcoming Assembly of States Parties, including its diplomatic approach to addressing US sanctions against the court. "Discussions are currently taking place about the diplomatic track being pursued," Berendsen said. "I cannot anticipate which subjects are or are not on the table." He added that the Netherlands could not decide the matter alone, because more than 120 member states would potentially have to reach an agreement with the US.

'All kinds of discussions are taking place, but that does not mean that this is the position the Netherlands is taking' – Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen "So the minister is not denying that it is true," Van der Werf responded. "All kinds of discussions are taking place, but that does not mean that this is the position the Netherlands is taking," Berendsen said. ICC member states are scheduled to meet in The Hague from 30 November to 7 December, after the session was relocated from New York because US sanctions and visa restrictions threatened participation.

Washington imposed sanctions on the ICC as an institution on 9 October, escalating a campaign that had already targeted most of the court's judges and prosecutors. The sanctions have been imposed since February last year, in the aftermath of the arrest warrants issued by the court for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant in November 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza .

In the institutional sanctions, Washington granted a six-month exemption for certain operational transactions to allow time for negotiations, with its expiry on 7 April next year. US sanctions International Criminal Court hours after former judge wins Nobel Peace Prize court from conducting transactions in US dollars, effectively cutting it off from large parts of the international financial system and potentially crippling its operations.

Banks tend to over-comply with sanctions because of their dependence on that system. Any agreement to rewrite the court's core powers would face substantial legal hurdles. Under the Rome Statute’s general amendment procedure, adoption requires consensus or a two-thirds majority, followed by ratification by seven-eighths of member states before entry into force. The reported discussions echo demands previously reported by Middle East Eye.

In December 2025, MEE revealed that Washington had pressed for an end to the Palestine and Afghanistan investigations and treaty changes preventing prosecutions of nationals of non-member countries, in return for lifting sanctions. Three diplomats familiar with the matter said an EU diplomat had presented the US demands to representatives of ICC member states ahead of the annual gathering of the Assembly of States Parties.

The assembly ultimately reaffirmed the treaty’s integrity. One diplomat warned that amendments intended to appease Washington could damage the court more than sanctions themselves. Restrictions on prosecutions The Rights Forum reported three potential restrictions that would fundamentally alter the court’s ability to prosecute international crimes. The first would grant immunity to heads of state and government.

The second would exclude nationals of non-member countries from the court’s jurisdiction, even for crimes committed on the territory of a member state. That would threaten the legal basis for prosecutions of Israeli officials over crimes in occupied Palestine. Israel has not joined the Rome Statute, but Palestine has, allowing the court to exercise territorial jurisdiction. The third reported restriction concerns complementarity: the principle under which the ICC acts when national authorities fail to genuinely investigate or prosecute.

According to The Rights Forum, the proposed change could allow the existence of domestic legislation criminalising relevant conduct to block ICC proceedings, even without genuine national investigations. In its response to the organisation, the Dutch foreign ministry said no concrete proposals were currently before the Assembly of States Parties, the court’s governing body. ICC confirms Middle East Eye reporting on Afghanistan arrest warrants w and with respect for the court’s independence and impartiality.

Rights groups and legal experts have repeatedly urged the EU to activate its Blocking Statute , a legal mechanism which aims to protect EU companies and individuals from the effects of extraterritorial sanctions imposed by third countries. If activated, the statute would reassure EU-based service providers that their transactions with the ICC are protected. It essentially prohibits them from complying with foreign laws that could harm their business operations within the EU.

Dutch and European leaders have pledged support but remain cautious about invoking the mechanism. Prime Minister Rob Jetten promised last month to protect the court “brick by brick”, while Berendsen has described the Blocking Statute as a drastic measure that could be used only once. EU leaders subsequently called for measures to help European companies continue serving the court. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said on 20 October that activating the statute remained an option, but required careful preparation.

She also urged companies against over-compliance with US restrictions during the six-month transition period. Established in 2002, the ICC is the world’s only permanent international criminal court with the mandate to investigate and prosecute individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression. The court currently has over a dozen active investigations , including the situations in Darfur, Libya , Myanmar and Ukraine .
