articles.body:
Finland says it will restrict entry to the country for Russian athletes because of the war in Ukraine, potentially affecting a number of winter sports. The move follows a backlash in Finland to Russia being reinstated for the ice hockey world championships.

“As long as Russia’s war of aggression continues, Russian athletes have no business in Finland,” said Elina Valtonen, the Minister for Foreign Affairs. “Their entry into the country would be a threat to Finland’s international relations. The same is true of other short-term work under visas that is not essential to Finland’s national interests.”

The Finnish foreign ministry said the measure would affect Russians competing under neutral status as well as those competing for national teams.

Finland hosts a figure skating grand prix next week and a cross-country ski World Cup this month. Both sports allow Russians to compete as “neutral athletes”. One major event to be affected is the figure skating world championships in March. Russian skaters are expected to be among the top medal contenders.

The International Skating Union (ISU) said it “has taken note of the statement today by the Finnish government related to Russian nationals entering the country and the possible consequential impact on sporting events, including the ISU figure skating world championships due to be held in Tampere, Finland, and is studying its implications”.

“ISU believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing.” The ISU added it was “seeking clarifications” from skating officials in Finland.

The change takes effect from Monday, so should not affect this week’s NHL games in Helsinki between the Seattle Kraken and Carolina Hurricanes or scheduled ski World Cup slalom races in Levi on Saturday and Sunday.

Finland is among a group of European teams to have vowed not to play against Russia at the ice hockey world championships. The men’s championships are scheduled for Germany, which is weighing up whether to go ahead with hosting.

In the longer term, Finland is due to host the European track and field championships in 2030. World Athletics, the sport’s governing body, maintains a blanket ban on Russian participation, though that is facing a legal challenge.

articles.title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills six Palestinians, health ministry says
articles.summary: Witnesses say a missile hit a building containing the surgical wards and intensive care units at Nasser hospital, the largest in southern Gaza.
articles.preview: Six people have been killed and about 30 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says. The hospital's director said two missiles hit a building containing surgical wards and intensive care units overnight, but that one of the missiles did not explode. The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".
articles.body:
Six people have been killed and about 30 injured in an Israeli air strike on Nasser hospital in the southern Gaza Strip, the Hamas-run health ministry says.

The hospital's director said two missiles hit a building containing surgical wards and intensive care units overnight, but that one of the missiles did not explode.

The health ministry said medical staff, patients and companions were killed, among them surgeon Dr Rizq Abu Shaira. It condemned the attack as a "flagrant violation of international laws and conventions".

The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas's armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a "headquarters" to plan attacks on its forces.

Hamas said that Israel was spreading "false narratives" in a "blatant attempt to cover up a new war crime".

Under international law, hospitals have a protected status, but they have been repeatedly targeted during the Gaza war.

Israel accuses Hamas, which retains security control of parts of Gaza not occupied by Israeli troops, of cynically exploiting civilian infrastructure. It says the group stores weapons and runs command and control rooms in hospitals, which Hamas denies.

Israel does not allow international news organisations, including the BBC, into Gaza, making it difficult to verify what is happening in the territory.

The Nasser Medical Complex is located in the city of Khan Younis and is the largest hospital in southern Gaza, serving almost one million people.

In a video posted on social media, a paramedic from the Hamas-run Civil Defence agency who arrived at the building after the strike early on Thursday said a missile penetrated the five-storey structure and hit a room in the surgical department.

Other footage shared by activists showed thick smoke inside the building and extensive destruction on the second floor, where medical equipment and beds had been scattered by an explosion.

The hospital's director, Dr Ahmed al-Fara, later told a news conference that Israeli forces had fired two missiles at the al-Yasin surgery building but that only one exploded.

"What's happened in Nasser Medical Complex is targeting the health sector mainly. We are talking about doctors, we are talking about civilians, we are talking about patients," he said.

"Also, there is... huge damage [to] the infrastructure inside the hospital."

Footage filmed by a freelance journalist working for the BBC showed extensive damage to an operating theatre, wards and a sleeping area for medics, as well as hallways and lifts.

News agencies also published photos that appeared to show an unexploded missile.

Dr Mohammed Qdeih, a general surgery specialist who was wounded in the head, said he and other medical staff had just finished work around 00:30 and had been preparing to go to sleep when there was an explosion.

"My whole body was trapped under the rubble. For a moment, I felt as if I was about to lose consciousness, or that I was about to die," he told the BBC.

"I started struggling to free myself and started calling out, 'Guys! Guys!' I began crawling, trying to pull my leg out from beneath the rubble. I managed to pull myself free. It was dark, there were no lights, nothing at all."

He said he had been lying in a bed near Dr Rizq Abu Shaira, who was killed. Another colleague suffered a broken leg.

"Dr Rizq was the kindest person in this department. He was very kind and always willing to help... And of course, he was a surgeon, one of the best among us."

He added: "Patients were killed as well. There were patients in the rooms next to us who were killed. A patient comes to the hospital seeking treatment and leaves carried on people's shoulders. I do not know what kind of humanity this is."

The Israeli military said in a statement that its "precise strike" had targeted the commander of Hamas's Khan Younis Brigade, who it named as Mohammed Abu Ismail, alongside other fighters who were "hiding inside" Nasser hospital.

"The terrorists were struck in order to remove the threat they posed after turning the Nasser hospital compound into a headquarters and operating from there to advance dozens of terrorist plots against our forces and restore the brigade's force," it alleged.

The military added that it had issued advance warnings before the strike and released an audio recording of what it said was one given to a senior Gaza health official. But Fara insisted the hospital had received no warning of an attack.

A Hamas statement rejected the Israeli military's accusations, calling them "a blatant attempt to justify a documented crime targeting a civilian medical facility whose function and purpose are well known".

"The nature of the targeted site and the casualties inflicted on patients, doctors and medical staff expose the falsity and weakness of this narrative," it said.

However, local activists circulated claims overnight that the strike may have targeted a senior Hamas security figure who was hiding inside the building.

Fara said this was the seventh time that Nasser hospital had been struck during the war. In August 2025, a double Israeli strike killed 22 Palestinians, including journalists and health workers.

The World Health Organization (WHO) said it had documented a total of 1,056 attacks on healthcare in Gaza over the past three years, resulting in 1,010 deaths.

"Gaza's health facilities are lifelines for its people. They must be protected. They must never be militarized or attacked," warned Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the UN agency's director general.

Later on Thursday, at least four more Palestinians were reportedly killed in separate incidents in northern and central Gaza.

Medics said three were killed in Israeli air strikes in Gaza City, Jabalia and Deir al-Balah, while the fourth was killed by Israeli gunfire in Bureij refugee camp.

The Israeli military said it struck a "terrorist" in Deir al-Balah and another in Gaza City.

Israeli strikes on Gaza take place almost daily despite a US-brokered ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas in October last year.

More than 1,620 people have been killed in Gaza since then, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza over the same period.

The humanitarian situation in Gaza also remains dire and has recently deteriorated further as a result of heavy rains last weekend that reportedly flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced families.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,650 people have been killed in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title: Un neonato morto di freddo a Gaza, un raid colpisce un ospedale
articles.summary: Netanyahu e Eisenkot si incontreranno oggi
articles.preview: Un bimbo di nove mesi è morto per ipotermia nella tenda in cui la sua famiglia aveva trovato rifugio a Khan Younis, nel sud della Striscia di Gaza. Lo hanno riferito due fonti palestinesi, mentre crescono le preoccupazioni per l'arrivo dell'inverno. Un medico palestinese che ha esaminato il corpo del bambino, Kinan Ahmad Raqiq, ha dichiarato all'Afp, in condizione di anonimato, che il piccolo "è morto di freddo".
articles.body:
Un bimbo di nove mesi è morto per ipotermia nella tenda in cui la sua famiglia aveva trovato rifugio a Khan Younis, nel sud della Striscia di Gaza. Lo hanno riferito due fonti palestinesi, mentre crescono le preoccupazioni per l'arrivo dell'inverno. Un medico palestinese che ha esaminato il corpo del bambino, Kinan Ahmad Raqiq, ha dichiarato all'Afp, in condizione di anonimato, che il piccolo "è morto di freddo". Anche la Difesa civile, organizzazione di primo soccorso che opera sotto l'autorità di Hamas, ha confermato che il piccolo è deceduto dopo essere stato esposto a un "freddo intenso". La morte del bambino, che si chiamava Kinan Ahmad Raqiq, è avvenuta dopo le piogge torrenziali che sabato hanno colpito il territorio palestinese, allagando decine di migliaia di tende degli sfollati. Secondo i soccorritori palestinesi, cinque palestinesi, tra cui tre bambini, sono morti a causa del maltempo.

Un attacco israeliano ha ucciso sei persone e ne ha ferite circa 20 presso l'ospedale Nasser, nel sud di Gaza; lo ha riferito giovedì all'Afp un funzionario della protezione civile. L'esercito israeliano ha confermato l'attacco, dichiarando di aver preso di mira "un terrorista di alto rango di Hamas e altri terroristi dell'ala militare di Hamas" che operavano all'interno della struttura ospedaliera. La protezione civile della Striscia di Gaza - un'agenzia di soccorso che opera sotto l'autorità di Hamas - ha reso noto che i corpi delle vittime e oltre 20 feriti sono stati estratti da un edificio del complesso medico.

Netanyahu e Eisenkot si incontreranno oggi

Il primo ministro Benjamin Netanyahu e il leader di Yashar Gadi Eisenkot hanno pubblicato una nota congiunta in cui comunicano che si incontreranno oggi presso l'ufficio del primo ministro a Gerusalemme per un aggiornamento sugli sviluppi in ambito diplomatico e di sicurezza. All'incontro parteciperà anche il segretario militare del premier, il generale Guy Markizano.

Washington sought to give new momentum to peace efforts following two days of negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, held under U.S. auspices in the United Arab Emirates. articles.body:
Russia

Russian President Vladimir Putin met Thursday at the Kremlin with envoys from U.S. President Donald Trump for talks on the conflict between Russia and Ukraine. Washington sought to give new momentum to peace efforts following two days of negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, held under U.S.

auspices in the United Arab Emirates. These were the first direct talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials in nine months, as peace efforts had stalled this year. Although they had just concluded two days of negotiations between Russia and Ukraine in the United Arab Emirates—which ended Wednesday with an agreement on a large-scale prisoner exchange— but failed to yield any visible progress toward ending nearly five years of large-scale hostilities, U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff appeared determined to seize the opportunity and traveled directly to the Kremlin.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky warned European leaders on Thursday against discussions between the United States and Russia regarding a new security agreement for the continent.

articles.title: Ukraine says military Starlink disrupted again as US envoys meet Putin in Moscow
articles.summary: Later on Thursday, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will travel to Dublin to meet Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.
articles.preview: President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Ukraine's military is again facing "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv is struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones. It came as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, a day after the latest talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi. Zelensky told European leaders in Dublin that Ukraine was trying to clear up the Starlink situation with the American side.
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has said Ukraine's military is again facing "systematic" restrictions to Starlink's military-grade satellite service, Starshield, meaning Kyiv is struggling to intercept Russian jet-powered drones.

It came as US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, a day after the latest talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine wrapped up in Abu Dhabi.

Zelensky told European leaders in Dublin that Ukraine was trying to clear up the Starlink situation with the American side.

But he added "some things" were already clear: "If someone in America is making decisions that basically treat Ukrainian territory as if it is not Ukrainian, then this tells us where things are going."

He did not elaborate further.

Starshield was developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX company for government and military use. Along with Starlink, it has come to play a vital role in facilitating communication on Ukraine's front line.

A similar issue with connectivity affected the front line in late October and lasted about a week before it was fixed. It remained unclear who had ordered the temporary restrictions on Starlink services at the time, with US officials and SpaceX offering differing explanations.

Zelensky said the current disruption had been ongoing for several days and was "helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine".

- Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?

- Published25 October

Kushner and Witkoff are expected to travel to Dublin to meet Zelensky after their meeting with Putin.

Videos shared by Russian media on Thursday showed the US representatives disembarking a plane and being welcomed by Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev with handshakes and hugs.

Later, they headed to the Kremlin where they met Putin and three of his senior advisors.

In remarks broadcast by Russian media, Putin asked the US envoys to convey his "gratitude" to US First Lady Melania Trump for her involvement in last month's Kherson region ceasefire, which allowed for the evacuation of hundreds of civilians from the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.

The Russian president then proposed organising a similar five-day ceasefire for Kostyantynivka, a contested front-line Ukrainian city in the eastern region of Donetsk.

Kyiv disputes that Russia fully holds the town, and a truce could help Moscow's troops to make a final push to seize it.

"Considering that they brought in equipment and rotated troops in Oleshky under the guise of a humanitarian operation, it's clear what they want in Kostyantynivka," Ukrainian presidential adviser Dmitry Lytvyn said, adding that the details would need to be "clarified".

The separate in-person meetings with the Russian and Ukrainian presidents were only announced on Wednesday after two days of talks which were framed as centred around the postwar security architecture of Europe.

Nearly five years since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow shows no sign of backing down from its maximalist demands for sovereign Ukrainian territory and for Western countries to give up any future commitment to protecting Kyiv in case of further attacks.

On Thursday, Putin again repeated that the presence of foreign troops in Ukraine was "unacceptable" to Russia, and said Russia would like the Americans to engage with Europe "so that the Europeans can decide what they truly want: peace or war".

During the first years of the war, Europeans cut communications with the Kremlin and refused to engage with Russia directly.

However, in recent times many have grown concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin, and have been pushing for a seat at the negotiating table.

The talks in Abu Dhabi were led by the Americans and only included Russia and Ukraine, but Kushner said he and Witkoff would ask Putin to "give his blessing" to invite European representatives in future discussions - particularly with regards to the future configuration of their continent's security architecture.

Kushner also urged Europe to "identify one person to speak on their behalf" in the negotiations.

But the Russians have been opposed to the idea, citing Europe's support for Kyiv as an obstacle.

Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation in Abu Dhabi, said he thought all parties had "moved closer to achieving peace" but that now "a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the United States, and on whether Europe comes to its senses".

articles.title: Allarmi bomba nelle scuole, Meloni incontra le opposizioni: "Appello all'unità". Schlein: ...
articles.summary: AGI - I leader delle opposizioni sono usciti da Palazzo Chigi , al termine dell'incontro con la premier Giorgia Meloni , con una linea unitaria: pronti a collaborare per arginare gli attacchi cyber, ma " nessuna delega in bianco al governo". La premier, arrivando poi al vertice della comunità europea a Dublino, ha giudicato "non concrete" anche le minacce pervenute alle scuole oggi nella seconda giornata di ondate di mail. Al tavolo, richiesto da Meloni dopo gli allarmi bomba recapitati con una mail in oltre 6mila plessi scolastici, siedono anche i ministri competenti per materia, Guido Crosetto e Matteo Piantedosi , i vice premier Antonio Tajani e Matteo Salvini e Alfredo Mantovano , sottosegretario alla Presidenza del Consiglio e Autorità delegata per la sicurezza della Repubblica. Le dichiarazioni della Premier "Abbiamo ritenuto che la minaccia non fosse una minaccia concreta e quindi abbiamo, per il tramite dei prefetti , del ministero degli Interni e dell' Istruzione , dato ai presidi , l'indicazione di non evacuare e chiudere le scuole ". Così la premier Giorgia Meloni , parlando degli allarmi bomba negli istituti scolastici prima di prendere parte al vertice della Comunità politica europea a Dublino. La premier ha ricordato che oggi pomeriggio si terrà una riunione del Cisr per individuare i protocolli specifici di comportamento . Protocolli sugli allarmi nelle scuole Riguardo gli allarmi nelle scuole la presidente del Consiglio ha poi sottolineato come "alcuni presidi avevano già provveduto" alle evacuazioni "ma nella giornata di oggi non abbiamo considerato che quelle mail fossero effettivamente una minaccia. Abbiamo deciso di procedere così. Puntiamo ad avere dei protocolli su questo", ha concluso. Confronto con l'opposizione sulla cybersicurezza Con l' opposizione "abbiamo condiviso le informazioni che avevamo. Abbiamo dato l'immagine, che è necessaria in questo momento, di una classe dirigente che al di là delle molte divisioni che la animano quando arriva il momento è capace di mettere da parte queste divisioni". Lo ha detto la premier Giorgia Meloni parlando prima del vertice della Comunità politica europea della riunione con i leader dell'opposizione sul tema della cybersicurezza . Caos scuole, Meloni chiama le opposizioni a Palazzo Chigi Al completo le opposizioni: Elly Schlein , Giuseppe Conte , Nicola Fratoianni e Angelo Bonelli , Matteo Renz i, Riccardo Magi , Carlo Calenda ed Edoardo Ziello in rappresentanza di Roberto Vannacci, rimasto a Bruxelles per la plenaria del Parlamento europeo. La premier, in via preliminare, ribadisce l' appello all'unità di tutte le forze politiche e assicura che l'appuntamento non vuole sostituire l' informativa al Parlamento richiesta dalle opposizioni. Il sospetto che circola nel campo progressista Poi lascia la parola ai leader del centrosinistra per raccoglierne le proposte. "Ma si tratta di un compito che non spetta a noi", dice Giuseppe Conte . Il sospetto che circola nel campo progressista è che Meloni, "fiutando di poter pagare pegno per gli allarmi di ieri", voglia condividere "la responsabilità per dire: anche le opposizioni sono d'accordo con me", spiega uno dei leader della coalizione. D'altra parte, come spiega anche Schlein in Transatlantico, poco dopo la fine della riunione, "la responsabilità dell'ordine pubblico e della sicurezza è del governo, non delle opposizioni. Facciano delle proposte e ne discuteremo in Parlamento ". articles.title: 10 Palestinians killed since dawn
articles.summary: 10 Palestinians killed since dawn Al Jazeera reports that 10 people have been killed in Israeli attacks across Gaza since dawn, including two strikes on hospitals which killed at least seven people. A deadly overnight strike on the Nasser Medical Complex in Khan Younis killed six people, including surgeons and patients, while at least one death was reported after a separate attack near the entrance to Gaza City's al-Shifa Hospital. Al Jazeera said that multiple casualties were also reported after an Israeli drone struck a vehicle south of Deir al-Balah in central Gaza. Meanwhile, Wafa news agency reports three deaths following the initial six in the Nasser Hospital attack. According to the report, Hossam Ali Saleha was killed in a strike targeting a vehicle outside the entrance to al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City. In Deir al-Balah, an Israeli drone struck a vehicle in the city's south, killing 26-year-old Nashat Fouad Awwad. In northern Gaza, another Palestinian was killed and several others wounded by Israeli fire targeting a group of people near Jabalia al-Nazla Cemetery.

articles.title: Supermedia AGI/Youtrend: campo largo ancora avanti al centrodestra
articles.summary: AGI - Per una strana coincidenza, nell’ultima settimana è stata pubblicata una quantità decisamente fuori dal comune di sondaggi sulle intenzioni di voto nazionali. Basti pensare che tra giovedì 5 e venerdì 6 novembre ben sei istituti demoscopici hanno pubblicato le proprie stime, ciascuno su un diverso canale. Nel complesso, questa sovrabbondanza di sondaggi - in totale 12 nel periodo considerato - rende la Supermedia di oggi particolarmente “robusta”. Una solidità che, peraltro, consente di verificare con molti più dati a disposizione le ipotesi emerse la scorsa settimana, in particolare a proposito di due forze politiche: Movimento 5 Stelle e Futuro Nazionale. Ci eravamo chiesti se il rimbalzo positivo di questi due partiti fosse il segnale di una tendenza effettivamente in atto oppure il frutto di un “miraggio statistico” . La risposta emerge molto chiaramente dai numeri di oggi: in un contesto generale che vede quasi tutte le forze politiche in lieve arretramento, le due maggiori eccezioni sono costituite proprio da M5S e FN. Il partito di Conte, in particolare, guadagna oltre un punto in due settimane, apparentemente senza nuocere al suo principale competitor interno, ossia il Partito Democratico. Appare chiaro che nelle scorse settimane il posizionamento tra gli elettori del M5S si è in qualche misura rafforzato, tornando su valori visti nei mesi successivi al referendum costituzionale. Il caso di FN è altrettanto interessante. Nelle scorse settimane avevamo rilevato come il partito di Vannacci si fosse evidentemente messo alle spalle il suo momento migliore, e come fosse in corso un “riflusso” di elettori verso il centrodestra - in particolare verso Fratelli d’Italia. I dati odierni (con diversi sondaggi che vedono FN ancora sopra il 7%) ci dicono però che il consenso verso Vannacci non è evaporato , e che il suo partito conserva ancora una quota di consenso non trascurabile con cui fare i conti. L'analisi sulle coalizioni Le due dinamiche appena viste si ripercuotono in modo evidente sugli equilibri tra le coalizioni. Se da un lato il campo largo riguadagna terreno, in primis grazie alla crescita del M5S, il recupero di Vannacci “tarpa le ali” alla rincorsa del centrodestra, che sembra aver esaurito la spinta dell’ultimo periodo, sia a causa dell’arretramento di FDI (che perde quasi mezzo punto nelle ultime due settimane) sia per l’esaurimento dell’effetto novità causato dall’ingresso in coalizione di Sud chiama Nord, che rimane stabile intorno all’1%. In attesa di capire se il Partito Liberal Democratico aderirà al centrodestra (nella sua interezza o con il solo Marattin in seguito a una probabile scissione), il divario tra le due principali coalizioni si allarga così a poco più di due punti percentuali. Attenzione però: i numeri di oggi non possono essere considerati come una diretta conseguenza di due importanti fatti politici degli ultimi giorni. Il primo è l’intensificarsi di attacchi informatici nell’ambito della cosiddetta “guerra ibrida”, elemento ormai innegabile che condizionerà la politica italiana nelle prossime settimane (a dir poco). Il secondo è la presentazione, da parte del Governo, della manovra di bilancio, che comprende una lunga serie di misure di cui è stata già testata la popolarità. E i risultati, in certi casi, sono sorprendenti. Secondo il sondaggio Youtrend per @SkyTG24 di oggi, la misura della legge di bilancio che raccoglie più consensi è l’esenzione permanente dal bollo per le auto fino a 80 kW e per le moto: la giudica positivamente il 62% degli italiani. https://t.co/urDNT5UL0d — Youtrend (@you_trend) November 11, 2026 Secondo il sondaggio Youtrend per Sky TG24, la misura più popolare tra quelle proposte (con il 62% di giudizi positivi) risulta l’esenzione del bollo auto, che diventerebbe strutturale e non più una tantum per il solo 2027; al secondo posto (56% di approvazione), il contributo INPS di 100 euro l’anno per i nuovi nati fino al compimento del 18° anno; le misure più impopolari, invece, sarebbero quelle relative al taglio delle assunzioni di personale nelle scuole (bocciato dal 72%) e l’aumento degli stanziamenti per le missioni militari all’estero (60% di contrari). C’è da dire che le ultime due misure citate sono anche le uniche a risultare impopolari anche tra gli elettori di centrodestra, mentre la proposta più “divisiva” è l’innalzamento a 100.000 della soglia di fatturato per il regime forfettario delle partite IVA (dove il saldo positivo è di 37 punti per chi oggi voterebbe per il centrodestra e negativo di ben 46 punti tra gli elettori del campo largo). Cosa dice la Supermedia della manovra Nel complesso, la manovra suscita poco entusiasmo: solo il 13% degli italiani ritiene che essa produrrà un effetto positivo sul proprio bilancio familiare, mentre il 28% prevede un effetto negativo e ben il 39% ritiene che non vi sarà alcun impatto. Sembra quindi che questa manovra, che sarebbe l’ultima ad essere approvata da questo Parlamento, non sia in grado di spostare la bilancia dei giudizi in modo particolarmente favorevole al Governo. Ma lo stesso sondaggio Youtrend rileva come tra gli italiani sia ancora il centrodestra a prevalere nella percezione legata alla capacità di gestione dell’economia, con un 26% a fronte del 21% del campo largo: ma qui bisogna notare soprattutto come il 40% dichiari di non fidarsi di nessuna di queste due coalizioni , in ambito economico. Come le recenti mid-term USA hanno insegnato, l’economia potrebbe essere il terreno su cui molti elettori orienteranno le loro scelte. Ma al momento, a differenza di quanto visto negli States, nessuno dei due principali contendenti sembra partire avvantaggiato in questa particolare arena. NOTA: La Supermedia Youtrend/Agi è una media ponderata dei sondaggi nazionali sulle intenzioni di voto. La ponderazione odierna, che include sondaggi realizzati dal 29 ottobre all’11 novembre, è stata effettuata il giorno 12 novembre sulla base della consistenza campionaria, della data di realizzazione e del metodo di raccolta dei dati. I sondaggi considerati sono stati realizzati dagli istituti EMG (data di pubblicazione: 5 novembre), Eumetra (5 novembre), Ipsos (31 ottobre), Ixè (11 novembre), Noto (5 novembre), Only Numbers (31 ottobre e 6 novembre), Piepoli (6 novembre), SWG (2 e 9 novembre), Tecnè (5 novembre) e Youtrend (11 novembre). La nota metodologica dettagliata di ciascun sondaggio considerato è disponibile sul sito ufficiale www.sondaggipoliticoelettorali.it.

La ponderazione odierna, che include sondaggi realizzati dal 29 ottobre all’11 novembre, è stata effettuata il giorno 12 novembre sulla base della consistenza campionaria, della data di realizzazione e del metodo di raccolta dei dati.

articles.title: UK court finds two Iranian men guilty of spying for Iran
articles.summary: The pair were promised rewards to send intelligence back to Iran, while one was prepared to commit a 'violent attack'.
articles.preview: The pair were promised rewards to send intelligence back to Iran, while one was prepared to commit a ‘violent attack’. Two Iranian men have been found guilty of spying for Tehran by a court in the United Kingdom after being accused of conducting surveillance on several people, including journalists for a Persian-language broadcaster in London.
articles.body:
The pair were promised rewards to send intelligence back to Iran, while one was prepared to commit a ‘violent attack’.

Two Iranian men have been found guilty of spying for Tehran by a court in the United Kingdom after being accused of conducting surveillance on several people, including journalists for a Persian-language broadcaster in London.

Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, were convicted on Thursday following a six-week trial at Woolwich Crown Court in south London for engaging in conduct likely to assist Iran’s intelligence service in a bid to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.

These included journalists for Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founding member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner. Iran International is banned by the government in Tehran.

A third defendant, Shapoor Qalehali Khani Noori, 57, was acquitted on all charges.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was outlawed by the UK in July under new powers to counteract state threats, with penalties of up to 14 years in prison for anyone convicted of supporting or assisting the organisation.

“This was a calculated operation to spy on those critical of the Iranian regime,” Frank Ferguson, chief prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service’s special crime and counterterrorism division, told reporters.

He said the pair were promised rewards to send intelligence back to Iran, while Sepahvand was willing to go beyond surveillance to commit a “violent attack” against at least one of the targets.

London’s Metropolitan Police said this was the fourth case in recent years involving direct threats to Iranian journalists in the UK and that it is “working hard to keep them safe”.

“The threat from hostile states to the UK is increasing and Iran continues to adapt its approach to using ‘proxies’,” said Vicki Evans, deputy assistant commissioner at the Met.

“We have seen examples where people who fly into the country to carry out criminal activity and then leave shortly afterwards, others where they use British nationals or, in this case, Iranian nationals with settled immigration status,” she added.

Most recently, Iran has been linked with a plot against a United States-run military airbase in England.

Sepahvand and Manesh were accused of visiting addresses linked to their targets, taking photos and videos and using platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online.

The pair will be sentenced at London’s Central Criminal Court, better known as the Old Bailey, on December 17.

articles.title: Mississippi elects first Black US Senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction
articles.summary: The US state of Mississippi has made history - electing its first Black Senator in 150 years and its first Democratic Senator since 1982. Forty-three-year-old Scott Colom narrowly beat incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith marking a seismic shift for the conservative southern state.
articles.preview: The US state of Mississippi has made history - electing its first Black Senator in 150 years and its first Democratic Senator since 1982. Forty-three-year-old Scott Colom narrowly beat incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith marking a seismic shift for the conservative southern state.
articles.body:
USA

Democratic nominee Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith on Wednesday in Mississippi's closely contested US Senate race after a prolonged ballot counting process, giving the state its first Black US senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.

Colom's narrow victory is a seismic shift in Mississippi, which has been controlled mostly by white conservatives for generations despite having the largest share of Black residents of any US state. The outcome adds to a decisive midterm rebuke of President Donald Trump, whose party suffered defeats in several Republican-controlled states, and it will bolster some Democrats' argument that their future runs through the American South.

“All I did was have the courage to imagine a night like this,” Colom told a crowd of hundreds who gathered at Tougaloo College for his victory party. “I had the courage to believe in Mississippi. I had the courage to understand that we can show the country that Mississippi matters.”

The Associated Press called the race in Colom's favor after local officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.

The last time Mississippi chose a new Democratic senator was 1947; the winner was a staunch segregationist. Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor, capitalised on the state's large Black population, discontent with the economy and Hyde-Smith’s missteps as she sought a second full term.

“They actually deserve a senator that will listen to them, that actually cares about what they think, actually cares about what they’re going through,” Colom said in the campaign's closing stretch.

Hyde-Smith, 67, called Colom late Wednesday afternoon to concede and released a concession speech online shortly afterward.

“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.”

Colom said during the campaign that he could represent all of Mississippi, a state where racial divisions have long defined its politics and society, and he repeated that pledge after his victory.

“My commitment to you, each and every one of you, is that first I’m going to treat your children like I want my children to be treated,” Colom said. “I’m going to treat your parents the way I want my parents to be treated. I’m gonna treat your future the way I want my future to be” and “work to make every Mississippian’s life better.”

Colom called on Mississippi's history

The senator-elect concluded his campaign with an ad that featured him at the Jackson home of Medgar Evers, the civil rights leader who, in 1963, was gunned down in his driveway by a white supremacist.

Colom told the story of Evers' military service at Normandy in World War II, his voter registration efforts in Mississippi, his assassination and the three decades it took to win a conviction. “He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honour everyone who died for that right.”

At the lectern Wednesday night, Colom said it was appropriate that the race be called on Veterans Day, as he again paid tribute to Evers.

“He served his country, came home to Mississippi, and they wouldn’t let him vote,” Colom said. “But he had faith that Mississippi could make progress."

articles.title: ‘No war, no peace’: Can Iran break the deadlock with the US?
articles.summary: Sustainable stalemate or slow-motion strangulation? The current 'equilibrium' is inherently unstable, experts say.
articles.preview: Sustainable stalemate or slow-motion strangulation? The current ‘equilibrium’ is inherently unstable, experts say. As the United States-Iran war drags on and talks remain stalled, Tehran is determined to move beyond a state of “no war and no peace”, parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has told Al Jazeera. Iran continues to assert control over which vessels may pass through the Strait of Hormuz, where attacks on tankers taking “unauthorised” routes have disrupted shipping.
articles.body:
Sustainable stalemate or slow-motion strangulation? The current ‘equilibrium’ is inherently unstable, experts say.

As the United States-Iran war drags on and talks remain stalled, Tehran is determined to move beyond a state of “no war and no peace”, parliament speaker and chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has told Al Jazeera.

Iran continues to assert control over which vessels may pass through the Strait of Hormuz, where attacks on tankers taking “unauthorised” routes have disrupted shipping.

Ghalibaf says Tehran remains open to a deal with the US to agree a ceasefire and the reopening of the strait, and has been waiting for Washington to respond to its terms for this to happen. “The ball is now in the American court,” he said.

Faced with the prospect of restarting an unpopular war or making concessions to Iran in order to secure a deal, experts say US President Donald Trump has for now chosen to ratchet up economic pressure. To this end, Washington has tightened sanctions, maintained its blockade on Iranian ports and announced an operation that Trump says will cut off overland routes Iran uses to transport advanced weapons and technology.

For now, full-scale fighting remains on hold, but a formal peace deal is still out of reach, with a fragile stalemate that may not hold for long, experts say.

“The current equilibrium is inherently unstable,” Ali Vaez, deputy programme director for the Middle East and North Africa at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera. “Because what Washington considers a sustainable stalemate, Tehran sees as a slow-motion strangulation. Both sides are banking on the other’s pain threshold being lower than their own.”

“That is a dangerous wager,” he added.

How long can Iran hold out?

Tehran has laid down seven conditions before it will agree to a ceasefire and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, then restart peace talks through a Qatari mediator, and has been waiting for an official US response to its demands. They include the lifting of the US naval blockade on Iranian ports, sanctions relief, releasing frozen Iranian funds, ending hostilities on all fronts and formally declaring the war over.

Ghalibaf said these conditions had already formed part of the memorandum of understanding (MoU) reached with the US in Islamabad in June and must be implemented before Iran will re-enter negotiations with the US.

But Tehran’s push for a deal reflects the pressure the blockade and sanctions are placing on its economy, analysts say. The longer that pressure lasts, the harder it may become for Iran’s leaders to agree to terms they may struggle to defend at home.

“Iran wants relief from the siege, but after paying such a heavy price … its leaders cannot afford a settlement that looks like surrender,” Vaez said. “The more Washington demands capitulation, the more elusive a deal becomes.”

But there are still signs of movement. Qatar said on Tuesday it was “working tirelessly” to resolve the crisis and that both sides had made positive statements about diplomacy. A day earlier, after hosting Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani at the White House, Trump said there was “momentum towards the end of this conflict”. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, however, has described Iran’s demands as “unacceptable”.

Gerd Nonneman, a professor of international relations and Gulf studies at Georgetown University in Qatar, told Al Jazeera that the cost of keeping up this pressure could narrow Washington’s room for manoeuvre.

“The US side may very temporarily think the status quo is preferable to making significant concessions now, but that will never be a sustainable strategy as it is prohibitively expensive, both in terms of overall economic effects and of the cost of the military operation,” he said.

Iran’s main source of leverage in the standoff is the Strait of Hormuz, analysts say. By seeking to dictate which ships can pass and which routes they can take, Tehran can raise the cost of the stalemate for Washington and its Gulf partners. Ghalibaf told Al Jazeera the waterway would “never return” to its pre-war status.

That leverage was on display last weekend, when shipping slowed sharply following attacks on tankers. Just five commodity vessels crossed on Saturday, November 7, while trade intelligence firm Kpler recorded none on Sunday, November 8. That compares with 31 crossings over the previous weekend, the Reuters news agency reported, citing the firm’s ship-tracking data.

In a statement carried by the Tasnim news agency, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said a “massive explosion” on Wednesday night brought two supertankers to a standstill as they travelled along a route it said was unauthorised. The IRGC said the vessels were carrying more than four million barrels of oil between them.

Analysts say intermittent attacks on tankers allow Iran to destabilise shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, preserving its main source of leverage over Washington.

“Washington has the luxury of waiting, but it does not have the luxury of deciding how Tehran behaves while it waits,” Vaez said. “The paradox is that the more effective America’s pressure campaign becomes, the greater Iran’s incentive to break the impasse by force.”

How long can Washington wait?

Trump’s advisers are reportedly divided over what to do next. Rubio has argued that the economic pressure campaign is working, while US Vice President JD Vance has pushed for a negotiated deal, according to Axios. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Trump’s adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner have backed maintaining economic pressure, the outlet reported.

“While neither would like to return to a state of war, I think the US is slightly more keen than Iran on the current stalemate, as a result of the economic pressure inflicted by the naval blockade,” Albert Vidal, of the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told Al Jazeera.

The US midterm elections last week could also affect Trump’s calculations. When the new Congress takes office in January, Democrats could use their newfound control over spending to make it harder for the administration to sustain military operations, Vidal said.

“At the same time, the Trump administration’s window to conduct major operations may be closing, too, as Democrats might choose to use the power of the purse in the new Congress in January,” he said.

Vidal said shortages of ballistic missile interceptors could push Washington to limit any renewed fighting.

Iran, meanwhile, has signalled that it may retaliate against civilian infrastructure as well as US military bases in the region, he said. A decision to resume hostilities could therefore draw Gulf countries further into a war whose economic and human costs they are already bearing.

“The tragedy is that both sides know how to start another round of hostilities, but neither knows how to control or end it,” Vaez said.

articles.title: Ukraine: Russian drone attack sparks major fire in Kyiv residential building
articles.summary: A Russian drone strike sparked a major fire at an apartment building in Kyiv, Ukraine, early on Thursday. Residents fled to safety as firefighters battled the flames and rescue workers helped people at the scene.
articles.preview: Flames engulfed part of a nine-storey residential block in Kyiv's Solomyanskyi district as thick black smoke billowed from shattered windows, with emergency crews battling to bring the blaze under control. Firefighters tackled the inferno while rescue workers evacuated residents and anxious onlookers gathered outside the damaged structure. From the sixth floor, one trapped resident desperately called out to crews below, pleading with them to extinguish the flames tearing through her flat.
articles.body: Flames engulfed part of a nine-storey residential block in Kyiv's Solomyanskyi district as thick black smoke billowed from shattered windows, with emergency crews battling to bring the blaze under control. Firefighters tackled the inferno while rescue workers evacuated residents and anxious onlookers gathered outside the damaged structure. From the sixth floor, one trapped resident desperately called out to crews below, pleading with them to extinguish the flames tearing through her flat. Amid thick smoke and extensive structural damage, firefighters continued their work as authorities assessed the scale of the destruction. A 44-year-old woman was confirmed dead and seven others injured in the attack, while the wider wave of strikes across Ukraine on 12 November claimed 10 lives in total.

articles.title: ‘Horrific crime’: Gaza doctor killed as Israel expands war on healthcare
articles.summary: Israel's military campaign and mass detentions collapse Palestinian healthcare in Gaza and the West Bank.
articles.preview: An unprecedented surge in military strikes and mass detentions has crippled medical infrastructure, leaving millions across the occupied territory without care. In the early hours of Thursday, Dr Rizq Abu Shuaira was on duty in the surgery department of the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza. An Israeli strike hit the hospital, killing at least six people, including Abu Shuaira and a child. Zaher al-Waheidi, spokesperson for the Ministry of Health in Gaza, on Thursday called it “a horrific crime”, adding that Israel targeted the surgery department.
articles.body:
An unprecedented surge in military strikes and mass detentions has crippled medical infrastructure, leaving millions across the occupied territory without care.

In the early hours of Thursday, Dr Rizq Abu Shuaira was on duty in the surgery department of the Nasser Medical Complex in southern Gaza. An Israeli strike hit the hospital, killing at least six people, including Abu Shuaira and a child.

Zaher al-Waheidi, spokesperson for the Ministry of Health in Gaza, on Thursday called it “a horrific crime”, adding that Israel targeted the surgery department. He called Abu Shuaira’s killing a loss to the medical profession in the enclave that’s struggling to cope with the large-scale destruction of health facilities since Israel launched its genocidal war on Gaza on October 7, 2023.

“The world woke up to the crime of targeting the Nasser Medical Complex,” al-Waheidi said, adding that Abu Shuaira was “martyred while on duty providing services to patients”.

“He did not deserve to meet his demise while among the patients in the hospital corridors,” he said.

Israel has repeatedly targeted Gaza’s medical personnel and hospitals in the past three years, killing at least 1,725 medical workers. Of the enclave’s 37 hospitals, 20 are partially functioning while 17 others have been rendered nonoperational. Health authorities say 44 percent of essential medicines are out of stock as Israel has continued to block the supply of medicines into the enclave of 2.3 million people.

Al Jazeera’s correspondent in Gaza said it was the seventh attack on the hospital, which serves at least 500,000 people in southern Gaza.

“Of course, this targeting led to widespread destruction inside the surgery departments and operating rooms, and led to major damage in the outpatient clinics, the radiology department and the laboratory department,” al-Waheidi told Al Jazeera.

Ruined hospital landscape

The Gaza Government Media Office stated that it holds Israel and the United States directly responsible for the strike on the hospital, noting that the victims included a 13-year-old child.

The media office has documented 793 Israeli attacks on healthcare services. A comprehensive report published last month by Insecurity Insight on ReliefWeb revealed that at least 3,508 attacks on healthcare across the occupied Palestinian territory were reported between October 2023 and September 2026. An overwhelming 95 percent of all incidents were attributed to Israeli forces.

In Gaza during that period, 399 health workers were detained, including Dr Husam Abu Safia, the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital, who has spent more than 500 days in Israeli custody.

“The Israeli occupation did not and will not stop targeting the health system,” al-Waheidi said.

Despite the so-called ceasefire signed between Hamas and Israel in October 2025, the Israeli attacks have not stopped in Gaza.

Expanded attacks in the West Bank

Israel has also been accused of expanding its attacks on medical infrastructure in the occupied West Bank. A World Health Organization report (PDF) covering hostilities from January to August 2026 documented 124 distinct attacks on healthcare in the territory. The WHO data confirmed four deaths and 40 injuries.

A subsequent monthly report issued by the Independent Palestinian Doctors Association (IPDA) in October 2026 painted a harrowing picture of escalating field violence. During October 2026 alone, the IPDA documented 23 violations against the healthcare system in the West Bank. Specific flashpoints highlighted in the report included Salfit Government Hospital, which was stormed by Israeli forces twice on October 14 to confiscate surveillance camera recordings, while a nearby ambulance centre was also violently raided.

Eid Dwaikat, media director of the Palestinian Red Crescent Society, shared with Al Jazeera the suffocating operational environment. “The work of the Red Crescent teams is in a highly dangerous and complex field environment, amid the continuation of the siege, closure, and restrictions imposed on movement and access to the affected areas, which constitutes a direct threat to the safety of paramedics,” Dwaikat said.

The human cost of these delays is measured in lives lost. “Preventing teams from reaching the injured and detaining them reflects directly on delaying the provision of life-saving first aid … which multiplies the risk of death or the exacerbation of critical injuries due to not receiving medical care in a timely manner,” he added.

Detained medical staff

The crisis has been vastly exacerbated by the systemic imprisonment of Gaza’s doctors. Physicians for Human Rights Israel (PHRI) has highlighted the plight of 14 detained Palestinian doctors, including hospital directors and specialised surgeons held without formal charges.

“Holding doctors for nearly two years under what is called the ‘Unlawful Combatants Law’ without pressing any charge and without trial … of course is incorrect,” al-Waheidi, the Gaza Health Ministry spokesperson, said.

“If the Israeli authorities have any evidence, they should present it in a fair public trial. But detention without charge and refusing independent medical examination under security pretexts is an arbitrary deprivation.”

Abu Safia, the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital, was detained in 2024, and his case has become emblematic of the systemic abuse within Israeli detention facilities.

On Wednesday, the PHRI said it obtained an independent medical review of Abu Safia’s records showing a weight loss of 14kg (31lb) in four months, a significant drop in haemoglobin levels and chest pain. On Wednesday, the Israeli Supreme Court dismissed a petition seeking his release and refused to allow an independent physician to examine him.

“In particular, we have documented and heard directly from the lawyer who visited Dr Husam Abu Safia, the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital: severe beatings, loss of consciousness, and a feeling by Dr Abu Safia that if this continues unchecked, his life is in danger,” Tirza Leibowitz, executive director of PHRI, told Al Jazeera.

“The torture and abuse have risen to such a level that we draw conclusions about this being a policy that has been implemented by the Israeli Prison Service against Palestinian detainees,” she said.

Leibowitz pointed out the plight of some 10,000 Palestinians held in Israeli detention under various categories. “The situation is appalling, both in terms of the conditions in the prisons and the violence and daily abuses that they are suffering,” she said.

A family’s agony

For the family of Abu Safia, the continued incarceration has been unbearable. Elias Abu Safia, his son, described the immense psychological toll of the prolonged separation.

“Unfortunately, we haven’t spoken with my father for the past 685 days. We only know about our father through the lawyer,” Elias told Al Jazeera. “We dream of being in touch with my father, to have a direct phone call with him. However, Israel is depriving us of having a direct conversation with my father.”

“The information that we are receiving about the health conditions of my father and how he is being arrested is very concerning. He doesn’t deserve to be treated that way inside or within the Israeli prisons,” Elias said.

articles.title: Le ipotesi sugli attentati criminali a Roma negli ultimi mesi
articles.summary: Nel quadrante est della capitale vari gruppi rivali si contendono il mercato della droga. Le bombe che hanno colpito attività commerciali e condomini sono un segnale del conflitto in corso
articles.preview: Casal Bruciato, periferia est di Roma. Dove prima c’era solo campagna, oggi sorgono palazzine di sei o sette piani costruite negli anni sessanta e settanta una accanto all’altra. articles.body:
Casal Bruciato, periferia est di Roma. Dove prima c’era solo campagna, oggi sorgono palazzine di sei o sette piani costruite negli anni sessanta e settanta una accanto all’altra. È qui che nella notte tra il 2 e il 3 novembre, intorno all’una, una bomba carta è esplosa nell’androne di un palazzo. Sono saltati i vetri fino al secondo piano. Venti minuti dopo – tra Torre Gaia e Tor Bella Monaca – una seconda esplosione ha danneggiato il portone e alcuni appartamenti di un edificio.

Si tratta degli ultimi due ordigni esplosi in pochi mesi nella capitale vicino ad attività commerciali, condomini, autolavaggi, autonoleggi e bar. Per Gianfranco Minissale, dirigente della squadra mobile di Roma, le bombe sarebbero diciannove e non sarebbero riconducibili a un’unica organizzazione. Alcuni episodi potrebbero essere collegati tra loro, altri sarebbero invece la conseguenza di ritorsioni e vecchie rivalità. “La bomba sta diventando una modalità criminale con cui risolvere qualunque tipo di problema”, ha osservato Minissale il 4 novembre in una conferenza stampa in questura.

Il quadrante orientale di Roma è da tempo uno dei territori più redditizi per il mercato della droga. Le piazze di spaccio sono una fonte di guadagno enorme per la criminalità organizzata e il loro controllo garantisce un flusso continuo di denaro, che viene investito in attività commerciali, sale giochi, usura.

La crisi del clan Senese

“Storicamente questo quadrante della città è egemonizzato dal clan Senese”, spiega Gianpiero Cioffredi, referente del Lazio dell’associazione Libera e autore di diversi studi sulla penetrazione della criminalità organizzata nella capitale. Per capire quello che sta succedendo bisogna ricostruire alcuni eventi importanti degli ultimi mesi e mettere in fila una serie di operazioni giudiziarie che hanno progressivamente modificato gli assetti criminali della città.

Il 18 marzo 2025 sono state arrestate 26 persone, tra cui Giuseppe “Peppe” Molisso e Leandro Bennato, considerati due importanti luogotenenti del clan di Michele Senese, con un ruolo nell’organizzazione delle piazze di spaccio.

Il 19 febbraio 2026 è arrivata la sentenza della cassazione nell’inchiesta Affari di famiglia, una delle principali indagini sugli interessi del clan. La sentenza ha sancito in via definitiva la natura mafiosa del clan guidato da Michele Senese. Sono diventate definitive le condanne per vari esponenti del gruppo tra cui la moglie del boss, Raffaella Gaglione, e il fratello, Angelo Senese.

Il 6 maggio 2026 un’altra operazione ha portato all’arresto di 18 persone nell’orbita dei Senese. Infine l’8 settembre 2026, con l’inchiesta Diabolik, sono stati ricostruiti anche gli accordi sul traffico di droga tra il clan Senese e la ’ndrangheta.

Il risultato di questa serie di successi giudiziari e investigativi, secondo Cioffredi, è un’organizzazione indebolita sia sul piano degli affari sia nella gestione del mercato degli stupefacenti. Ma avere assicurato alla giustizia i responsabili del traffico di droga a Roma non ha risolto il problema, in assenza di interventi potici strutturati. Ha invece creato un vuoto di potere che ora diversi gruppi criminali cercano di colmare.

Da quanto è emerso dalle indagini, per anni Molisso e Bennato hanno contribuito a organizzare un sistema costituito da circa 28 piazze di spaccio nel quadrante est della città. Le piazze erano gestite da gruppi locali, che mantenevano una certa autonomia, ma in cambio della protezione del clan compravano da questo la cocaina a prezzi superiori a quelli di mercato. Il clan interveniva nella risoluzione dei conflitti, nel recupero crediti e nella gestione dei rapporti tra le piazze. Un sistema che, secondo Cioffredi, arrivava a muovere circa tre tonnellate di cocaina al mese.

Con gli arresti e le condanne, quel sistema si è incrinato. “Si è aperto un conflitto per la gestione delle piazze di spaccio”, spiega l’esperto. Da una parte ci sono gruppi emergenti o organizzazioni che per anni sono rimaste ai margini e ora cercano di conquistare una posizione autonoma; dall’altra affiliati del vecchio sistema che tentano di conservare il controllo del mercato.

Tra i nomi che emergono dalle indagini c’è quello di Emanuele Selva, indagato e attualmente latitante, che secondo Cioffredi potrebbe essere una delle persone intenzionate a resistere alla ridefinizione degli assetti criminali della città.

La partita economica è enorme. Una piazza di spaccio, spiega Cioffredi, può fruttare tra i 15mila e i 40mila euro al giorno. Negli ultimi dieci anni, inoltre, il mercato romano della droga ha attirato anche gruppi criminali locali che in precedenza si occupavano soprattutto di rapine e altri reati. Le organizzazioni più strutturate, come la ’ndrangheta e la camorra, garantiscono l’importazione della cocaina, mentre la gestione delle piazze è affidata prevalentemente a gruppi del posto, ai quali negli ultimi anni si è aggiunta anche manovalanzadi origine straniera.

Già nel 2025, secondo Cioffredi, un intervento dei carabinieri aveva permesso di evitare un possibile regolamento di conti che avrebbe potuto provocare diversi morti. Ma ora le esplosioni rappresentano l’inasprimento di un conflitto già in corso. E a renderlo preoccupante è anche la facilità con cui ci si può procurare e costruire ordigni artigianali “fatti in casa” con materiali disponibili sul mercato.

Non è una guerra di mafia

Cioffredi invita però a non parlare di una nuova guerra di mafia come quella avvenuta in Sicilia negli anni ottanta. “Se ci fosse una guerra di mafia, ci sarebbero i kalashnikov o il tritolo”, afferma. “Se ci fosse una guerra di mafia, ci sarebbero i morti”.

Secondo l’esperto le grandi organizzazioni criminali come cosa nostra, la camorra o la ’ndrangheta non hanno intenzione di rompere i loro patti di non belligeranza su Roma. Se decidessero di farlo gli attentati sarebbero più violenti e non userebbero esplosivi artigianali. In questo caso invece si tratta di un conflitto tra gruppi locali rivali o tra gli stessi affiliati al clan Senese, che ora cercano di guadagnare autonomia e affrancarsi dall’organizzazione in un momento di crisi.

Roma è una città dove le organizzazioni criminali non si limitano a gestire il traffico di droga: investono e riciclano il denaro. E costruiscono relazioni con una parte dell’economia legale. Cioffredi richiama le migliaia di operazioni finanziarie sospette registrate negli ultimi cinque anni dagli investigatori e fa una stima del giro d’affari del riciclaggio nella capitale che, sulla base degli studi della Banca d’Italia, sarebbe pari ai tre miliardi di euro.

Si tratta di un “comitato d’affari virtuale”, in cui la criminalità organizzata è in buoni rapporti con una borghesia pronta a collaborare, fatta di imprenditori e professionisti compiacenti. Le mafie diventano fornitrici di servizi: fatture false, evasione dell’iva, recupero crediti, gestione dei conflitti sindacali. Un sistema che permette di trasformare i profitti illeciti in attività economiche e patrimoni legali.

Questo rende ancora più necessario un intervento delle istituzioni, che non può essere limitato solo ad azioni giudiziarie o di pubblica sicurezza. Per togliere terreno alle mafie è necessario fare degli investimenti economici, sociali, culturali. “I quartieri con la più alta penetrazione criminale sono quelli più poveri, perché lì le mafie rappresentano anche un’opportunità di lavoro, una fonte di guadagno”, spiega Cioffredi. Molti di quelli che hanno perso il reddito di cittadinanza, si sono messi al servizio della logistica criminale con il “sistema della retta”: in cambio di soldi “nascondono piccole partite di stupefacenti in casa o in cantina”.

Un fenomeno sottovalutato

L’interpretazione di Cioffredi è condivisa da Danilo Chirico, presidente dell’associazione antimafia Da Sud, impegnata da anni a monitorare la penetrazione criminale nella capitale. “La stragrande maggioranza delle intimidazioni e delle bombe erano dirette a un territorio e a persone che hanno a che fare con il mondo della droga e di Michele Senese”, spiega. Secondo Chirico, il conflitto potrebbe essere alimentato contemporaneamente da chi cerca di approfittare dell’indebolimento del clan per conquistare spazio e da chi vuole impedire che il vecchio sistema sia smantellato.

Tra i gruppi che aspirano a una maggiore autonomia ci sarebbero anche bande locali, composte in parte da giovani di origine tunisina e marocchina, che in passato avrebbero lavorato all’interno di questo sistema e ora punterebbero a gestire direttamente i propri affari. Organizzazioni criminali esterne, dunque, ma bande che vogliono liberarsi delle gerarchie precedenti.

Chirico individua un precedente nel periodo tra il 2010 e il 2012, quando a Roma c’era già stata una fase di forte instabilità intorno agli affari del gruppo di Senese, allora indebolito dalla detenzione del suo capo. Anche in quel caso, racconta, le persone coinvolte nelle intimidazioni erano in larga parte riconducibili al mondo dello spaccio. “L’aria che si respira mi ricorda quel periodo”. Oggi, come allora, la debolezza del sistema di comando sembra aver acceso le rivalità.

La sottovalutazione di questa presenza mafiosa preoccupa Chirico. “A Roma abbiamo una presenza criminale mafiosa dagli anni sessanta”, ricorda, citando anche la relazione della Commissione parlamentare antimafia del 1991, che già descriveva dinamiche oggi tornate al centro dell’attenzione.

Eppure ogni volta che le grandi inchieste fanno emergere organizzazioni strutturate e rapporti con l’economia legale, la città sembra scoprirle per la prima volta. Anche in passato, secondo Chirico, si è spesso preferito minimizzare, descrivendo le tensioni come piccole guerre tra bande, per il timore di indebolire l’immagine della città o danneggiarne le economie.

Il 14 ottobre Libera ha tenuto una manifestazione a piazza Roberto Malatesta, nel quartiere Prenestino, per denunciare la serie di bombe ed esplosioni con lo slogan: “Fuori le mafie da Roma”. All’evento sono intervenuti molti cittadini e autorità locali.

“Mi pare che ci sia un pezzo della società civile che comincia a preoccuparsi”, dice Chirico, il quale allo stesso tempo denuncia l’insufficienza della risposta politica e istituzionale. Le bombe sono il segnale più visibile di una crisi che covava da tempo. Ma il sistema che le rende possibili è molto più ramificato e per ora è sottovalutato da chi deve contrastarlo. ◆

articles.body:
An Israeli airstrike on Nasser hospital in southern Gaza killed six people, including a surgeon and a disabled man, and wounded 28 others, according to the hospital director.

The Israeli military carried out the attack on the hospital, in Khan Younis, early on Thursday saying in a statement it had struck a Hamas commander and other fighters there, without providing evidence.

The strike destroyed part of the surgery department, and caused extensive damage to several floors. Services were suspended in four departments: radiology, laboratories, surgical operations and inpatient surgical wards, according to Dr Ahmed al-Fara, hospital director.

The ceiling of one of the wards had caved in, while debris-covered beds lay next to medical instruments twisted from the force of the blast. In other rooms, piles of rubble and shattered concrete cluttered the floor and a hole was left in the floor, where the bomb penetrated the building.

Dr Ayman Abu Ubaid, a surgical specialist at Nasser medical complex, who was wounded in the attack, said: “The bombing caused thick smoke to fill the rooms and fires to break out, amid the groans of wounded and people’s screams. There were many casualties and blood everywhere … Most of us sustained injuries to our limbs, as well as shrapnel wounds in different parts of our bodies.”

Ubaid said the strike came at about 12.30am, without warning. “The patients in the department were all surgical patients waiting to undergo operations. The bombing happened at a time when they should have been asleep,” he said.

Among the dead was Rizk Abu Shaira, 52, a general surgeon who had featured in American Doctor, a documentary about doctors operating in Gaza.

“Dr Rizk was in the American Doctor documentary operating and serving his people. He lost his life doing that, he lost his life because he was doing that,” Dr Thaer Ahmad, who also featured in the documentary, posted on X.

Abu Shaira was killed alongside one of his patients, on whom he had operated.

Nasser hospital is one of the last functioning healthcare facilities in Gaza, after Israeli bombing made most of the strip’s facilities unusable. Last year Israel also struck the hospital, killing five journalists in a double-tap strike on a location often used by reporters for filming. In all, the hospital has been attacked seven times since the war on Gaza began.

The Israeli military has accused Hamas of using hospitals as command centres and to store weapons, an accusation the militant movement rejects. More than 1,700 healthcare workers have been killed in Gaza, while Doctors Without Borders (MSF) says Israel has detained hundreds of medics since 7 October 2023, with at least 95 still in custody.

About 90% of Gaza’s health infrastructure has been destroyed or damage by Israeli bombing, systematic destruction UN experts called “medicide”.

Attacking healthcare facilities and staff is illegal under international humanitarian law, though these facilities can lose their protected status if they are used for military purposes.

There is an increased need for healthcare during the winter months in Gaza, where rains have displaced people from their tents and increased communicable diseases in crowded encampments.

Already, Nasser hospital is lacking about 80% of its essential medicines and medical supplies, said al-Fara, its director.

One of those killed in Thursday’s strike was Seif Ghazi Abu Hatab, 29, who was admitted to Nasser hospital on Monday after a piece of debris fell on his back while he was helping clear rubble from a friend’s home. He was scheduled for surgery at 10am on Thursday, and was meant to receive further treatment abroad.

“Seif was a young man in the prime of his life. He wanted to live, rebuild his home and start a normal life, free from problems and suffering … Seif was killed after already losing two of his brothers and his father. His mother has now lost three of her sons,” said his cousin Tareq Abu Hatab, 37.

Israel launched the war in Gaza after the 7 October 2023 Hamas-led attack that killed about 1,200 people and took 251 hostage. At least 74,645 people have since been killed in Gaza and Israel has carried out a genocide in the strip, according to the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

Israel continues to carry out airstrikes in Gaza, killing more than 1,600 people since the October 2025 “ceasefire”, according to the Gaza ministry of health.

articles.body:
November 12, 2026

Israel says Hamas was using the hospital as a military command center, while Palestinian officials report at least six people killed, including a surgeon. The strike comes amid an increasingly fragile ceasefire.

Israel said it had targeted a senior Hamas member in a Gaza hospital in an overnight airstrike which reportedly killed six people.

According to the Israeli military, Muhammad Abu Ismail and other militants from the Islamist group had been operating a command center inside the Nasser hospital in Khan Yunis.

Gaza's civil defense service said at least six people were killed, including a surgeon and more than 20 were wounded. It said that parts of several floors were severely damaged or destroyed.

During war, hospitals are protected under international humanitarian law, although they can lose that protection if they are used for military purposes.

Israel says hospital used for terrorist activities

In a statement on Thursday, the Israeli military (IDF) said, without providing evidence, that Hamas was "operating within Nasser Hospital in Khan Yunis" and were using the complex "as a hub for military and terrorist activities against IDF troops and Israel."

The IDF identified the targeted senior Hamas member as Abu Ismail, adding he "was responsible for directing terrorist attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops and for holding numerous hostages captive throughout the war."

The IDF said the hospital was used for storing weapons, to conduct interrogation, operate command-and-control rooms as well as to shelter terrorists.

What happened at the hospital?

The Gaza Health Ministry said the Israeli airstrike hit the surgery department, killing six people including surgeon Rizk Abu Sharia.

News agency Reuters reported seeing footage from inside the hospital showing extensive damage with debris scattered around rooms and equipment.

Wounded people were also seen in the wreckage while several bodies were being carried away as firefighters worked to clear the scene.

Hamas has described the strike as a "fully-fledged war crime."

Since the beginning of the war in 2023, Israeli forces have attacked several hospitals in the Gaza Strip.

Fragile ceasefire

The war on Hamas in Gaza began in October 2023 after Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

Since then, more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, whose figures are generally considered reliable by the international community.

More than 1.6 million residents of Gaza's 2.1-million population now live in tents or other makeshift shelters due to Israel's war in the enclave.

A ceasefire came into effect in October 2025, but attacks have continued since then. While Israel says Hamas is trying to regroup, the Palestinian militant group says it's committed to the ceasefire and that Israel is trying to undermine the agreement.

Hamas is recognized as a terrorist organization by the EU, the US and several Arab states.
